title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Warhammer 40K Boltgun 2
content:
Three years ago, Auroch Digital dropped Boltgun, and all was good. Then last week Boltgun 2 was dropped, and all was even better. I purposefully hadn’t followed development for this game outside of what I saw from Warhammer Skulls. I prefer to go into things totally blind for my own sake, but deep down I knew I was going to enjoy this game no matter what.

I’m a sucker for Boomer Shooters, a slave to the genre really, the crazier the better, and Boltgun slots in on the tamer end of the spectrum where games like ULTRAKILL sit on the far other end.

Boltgun 2 is a lot more of the same formulae, and I mean that in a mostly positive way, except that it’s bigger, more refined, and just has a lot more stuff in it. It’s the same fun, you’re sprinting, jumping, charging, shooting, bashing, chopping through really cool arenas while the music team use your weapon noises as background percussion for their screeching guitar riffs.

Where the first game was jumping, chainsword charging and strafing, Boltgun 2 is all about more frantic, twitchy, high-speed carnage where you’re slide cancelling into a slo-mo superjump that lets you empty a Storm Bolter into some bozo in power armour and end his 10,000 year survival streak.

Departing from the first game, Boltgun gives you two characters to play with. I always thought they’d add more characters to Boltgun 1, it seemed set up for it, but it never happened. I don’t know if that was a scrapped plan or not, but they’ve made up for it here. Boltgun 2 pitches two badass heroes of the Imperium for you to play, the returning Sternguard Veteran Malum Caedo, (still voiced by Rahul Kohlui) and the Sister Celestian Nyra Veyrath. (Voiced by Alanah Pearce, who you'd recognise as Malevola from Dispatch!)

Promotional image courtesy of Auroch Digital.

You have different loadout options available to each character, with some crossovers, a different ability each that does the same thing (charging into enemies and making them explode), and a different health/armour pool. The Sister of Battle, Nyra, is generally faster and can jump higher, while Malum can tank more damage overall and has access to way quicker horizontal movement with his charge.

I don’t think there’s so much of a difference between the two that you feel like you’re missing out if you only play once, your mileage will really depend on how cool you find the weapons. But I really don’t think you’re going to play just once though.

The campaign for both characters is the same, but there’s a branching path system so there is a chance to do different levels as either character with the same convergence points through it all. It’s a nice way to make a playthrough of each character feel different, and there’s no weak points along the way either. All the levels kick some serious ass, and it makes hunting down Vashtorr as much fun the second time as it was the first.

The improvements they have made to the gameplay from the first game are small but impactful, like improving the controls to include a weapon wheel instead of relying on hotkeys, and your movement options being expanded to the point that Malum Caedo clearly missed his calling by choosing to be a Sternguard instead of a Vanguard Veteran. (seriously, he can leap across the map with his chainsword. and that's without a jump pack.)

If you’re speedrunning inclined, there is absolutely some heinous tech you can do to start beating levels in stupid quick time. Your level of freedom in leaping around, especially with the enhanced mobility in this game, means you’ll have plenty of fun trying to find skips. This isn’t im-sim levels of shenanigans by any means, it’s still a linear game, but I feel they found various ways players could skip parts of the level in development and just shrugged their shoulders at it.

In addition to Josh's review, Rob and Norman have been playing Boltgun 2 over on the Tabletop Battles YouTube channel:

Not that you want to skip past enemies because the new weapons added to the game are sick. Flamers in Boomer Shooters tend to be underwhelming, but Nyra's version of the flamer acts less like a traditional flamer and more like a pressure-washer of death. It was the most fun weapon to use in the game by far. The Meltagun as well has been revamped from a glorified super shotgun into my new favourite representation of a meltagun to date. It’s a solid beam that deals heavy pulses of damage that totally slag anything in front of you, and it only gets better when you get the multi-melta.

All the art they’ve made for the game is gorgeous, and there’s so much more of it this time around. Boltgun 1 had a limited enemy roster of Tzeentch and Nurgle Daemons, cultists, and Chaos Space Marines & Terminators. Boltgun 2 has the same, and then sprinkles on every Cult Legion for flavour.

You’ll be fighting Berserkers, Scarab Terminators, Noise Marines, Blightlord Terminators, and daemons you didn’t see in the previous game too, like Daemonettes and Bloodcrushers. It’s a lot. You won’t be doing it alone either, as a regiment from the Death Korp of Krieg pops up sometimes to help you out (by soaking up boltrounds, mainly).

Boltgun 2 has a much larger scope to its campaign. Boltgun 1 was set on Graia, a single planet, and there were a lot of fun environments to it but there had to be a unifying motif between levels. Boltgun 2 has you visiting multiple planets, different areas on those planets, voidships both Imperial and Chaos, and it let the level designers run absolutely wild.

There are some ridiculously cool environments in Boltgun 2, and it stands out as one of the things I loved most about the game. You need two playthroughs to appreciate them all, as there’s a branching mission path to accommodate two playthroughs with two different characters, but it’s so worth it. There’s some absolutely badass stand outs, like a Khornate Ziggurat with gore pits, industrial blood pumps, and so many piles of skulls that sit nicely against more traditional Imperium grimdark industrial, like an underwater lab facility or an underhive.

I don’t want to seem like all the new sprite work for enemies and allies didn’t excite me, it did, but the level design was just so fantastic I had to dedicate a big chunk of this review to call it out. Explore those levels. It’s worth it. (And they’re littered with secrets.)

Despite how cool it was to see all the legions in the game, I found the variety worked against the game. Boltgun 2 is a brisk experience; I got it done twice in about 12 hours on Hard mode. There’s a good chance you’ll only encounter a type of enemy for two campaign missions at most, and that sucks.

I think the game could really have benefited from some kind of Codex that stored enemies you encountered so you could read about their mechanics and check out their sprites up close. It’s a small gripe because it feels like a ‘my lobster too buttery, my steak too juicy’ type of complaint but I just liked some enemies more than others, and wanted to keep fighting them more.

This game is well worth a buy if you’re a fan of this genre, and a great first try if you’re Boomer Shooter curious. It’s a short, sweet, and gentle introduction to the craziness of this type of game. Obviously if you’re a Warhammer fan this game will speak to you on a lot of levels; the art, the story, the vibes are all immaculately Warhammer but if you’re just someone who wants a shooter, it’s totally sick. Is it a great intro to the setting? Not particularly, it doesn’t explain much, but it doesn’t need to.

I think it’s a shame it took three years to come out but hopefully they open a pipeline to get more content into the game, some DLCs, or some workshop support would be great. Games like this can live forever with a level editor, just look at what people are still doing with GZDoom.

For the price tag, I’d find it hard to regret picking it up. If you’re into replaying games, there’s a lot to do between trying harder difficulties, 100% secrets on both characters, and speedruning especially I think can be a massive draw for this game in particular. There are some great tools available to do skips and I’m excited to see people find them out.

If you’re someone who is one and done, I think you’ll be satisfied too. Getting to that final boss fight and hearing Mick Gordon make a guitar growl and snarl at you before you unleash all the weapons in your arsenal is more than satisfying one time over.

title: Detachment Focus: Veterans of the Long War (Updated October 19, 2026)
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Veterans of the Long War Detachment for the Chaos Space Marines.

The Tenth Edition release of Codex: Chaos Space Marines gave the faction access to a whopping eight detachments, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. These can dramatically change how the army plays, as each one tends to push players to build in a different way, even more so with the addition of force dispositions in 11th edition. In this series we’re diving deep into each Detachment and talking about what its rules are and how to play it. This article will be focusing on the Veterans of the Long War Detachment.

Changelog

  • October 19, 2026 (Current): Updated for 11th edition
  • November 11, 2025: Updated with new lists and tactics
  • January 9, 2025: Updated with errata, dataslate changes, and a new list
  • May 11, 2024: Initial Publication

Detachment Cost: 2 DP

Disposition: Take and Hold

Ostensibly designed to be the Black Legion Detachment for Chaos Space Marines, the Veterans of the Long War Detachment gives Chaos Space Marines players a taste of the old "Oath of Moment" army rule Space Marines had in tenth edition. It's a powerful rule that couples well with both the CSM army rule for LETHAL/SUSTAINED HITS and helps shore up the inconsistent performance you can get from units like Vindicators, Obliterators, and Havocs.

Power-wise Veterans of the Long War isn’t quite in the top tier of Chaos Space Marine options, but full re-rolls to hit are powerful and there are some strong abilities in the Detachment’s Stratagems and as it only costs 2 DP, you're left open to take Cabal of Chaos (yes) or one of the other two 1 DP options (pass). There are a number of units in the Chaos Space Marines army which really need re-rolls to hit to reach their full potential, and Veterans of the Long War lets them get there. You can build a perfectly competitive list using this detachment, even if you aren't one of the world's best players.

Detachment Rule: Focus of Hatred

At the start of your Command phase, select one unit from your opponent’s army to be the focus of your hatred. Until the start of your next Command phase, each time a HERETIC ASTARTES model from your army (excluding DAMNED models) makes an attack that targets your focus of hatred, you can re-roll the Hit roll.

Full re-rolls to hit are a powerful boost. This combines extremely well with Dark Pacts to let you fish for additional Sustained or Lethal Hits, and helps you focus down key targets without having it overcommit. It's particularly great for punishing elite armies relying on a small number of powerful units, such as knights or custodes. What’s also great about this is that, aside from a few key units we’ll mention, pretty much any unit can benefit from this, letting you keep your options open as you build your list.

If there’s a downside here it’s that the ability isn’t great for dealing with hordes of cheap models, and there are a number of units in your army which can already re-roll hits, such as Chaos Terminators. On that note it’s ironic that Abaddon’s aura to re-roll hits butts up against the core rule of his detachment (though it does free you up to use his 4+ invulnerable save more). That said, it’s only for one enemy unit, so don’t be afraid to take units which re-roll hits anyways, as you’re going to shoot/fight more than one thing per round most of the time.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

The Veterans of the Long War Enhancements are a mixed bag. They’re just okay, and not really things you’d build around. Warmaster's Gift is the one you'll end up including in most lists, but if you have the points, the Eye of Abaddon and Mark of Legend can each be worth taking.

  • Warmaster’s Gift (15 points) – Chaos Lord model only. Each time you make an attack that targets your focus of hatred an unmodified successful wound roll of 5+ scores a critical wound. This is good for one thing and that’s a Daemon Hammer Chaos Lord, where you can use it to score more Devastating Wounds, particularly in concert with the Chance for Glory ability to bump those to 3 damage. Pair him with Legionaries for re-rolls to wound and you’ve got an incredibly nasty melee threat.
  • Eager for Vengeance (20 points) – Goes on a non-DAMNED model. Your unit is eligible to Fall Back and shoot and charge. Additionally, if you fell back this turn, then each time your unit makes an attack that targets your focus of hatred you get +1 to hit, and each time you select your focus of hatred as the target of a charge you get +1 to the Charge roll. This is a really powerful effect, but the fact that it's all gated behind having to actually make a Fall back move makes this incredibly situational and a bit too expensive at 20 points. I'm sure there are times when you can use this but this is easily the least useful of the four options here and the fact that it costs 20 points is criminal.
  • Eye of Abaddon (15 points) – Goes on a non-DAMNED model. While the bearer is on the battlefield, each time the focus of your hatred is destroyed you roll a D6 and on a 4+ you get 1 CP. This is something I’d pay 5 points for, but at 15 it’s a bit too much. Chaos Space Marine armies often really want CP and have very few ways to get more of it, which can potentially make this a solid addition, but 15 points for a 50/50 shot at more CP is a bit too much, and Warmaster's Gift just gives you more power on a hammer Chaos Lord.
  • Mark of Legend (10 points) – Goes on a non-DAMNED model. Once per turn you can re-roll one hit roll, wound roll, or one saving throw for the bearer. The obvious place to put this is on a Daemon Prince, where the save is helpful for keeping him on the table and having an extra re-roll during the attack sequence (in addition to the one hit/wound re-roll you already get) is pretty great. It's also solid on a Lord Discordant and it’s also okay on a Hammer Chaos Lord. At 10 points is likely to be where you spend your last 10 if you end up short of 2000.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Stratagems

The Veterans of the Long War Stratagems are an interesting mix. One of them is absolutely amazing, to the point that you more or less always want 1 CP available to use it. The rest are mostly situational.

  • Endless Ire (Epic Deed, 2 CP) – Used when your focus of hatred is destroyed. Pick a visible enemy unit within 12” of one of your non-DAMNED character to become your new focus of hatred until your next Command phase. This one is very situational, requiring a lot of things to line up right but every now and then you’ll be able to use it to double up on hit re-rolls and surprise an opponent by finishing something off, then pivoting to a second big kill. It's very situational and expensive, and as a result something you're likely to use a Chaos Lord for to drop the cost to 1. The ideal scenario here is often going to be "shoot one target to death, then use this to nominate a second one you're about to charge."
  • Contemptuous Disregard (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Worsen the AP of incoming attacks by 1 for a phase on a non-DAMNED unit for a single activation. The Chaos version of Armour of Contempt is OK. It tends to do its best work in melee, where you're only having one unit throw hands into you, and can be really helpful for shrugging off high volumes of AP-1 attacks from bolters or chainswords.
  • Bringers of Despair (Epic Deed, 1 CP) – Used in the Fight phase. One non-DAMNED unit within Engagement Range of your focus of Hatred gains the Fights First ability. The changes to Fights First and fight order in 11th edition make this a lot less useful, as you'll always have to wait for a charging unit to fight before you can throw this out there - it basically acts as a 1 CP interrupt against your Focus of Hatred now. Still, that's not terrible, and you can get a lot of value out of it for 1 CP. It can be a way to deter your Focus of Hatred from charging something.
  • Black Crusade (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your Movement phase on a non-DAMNED Infantry or Mounted unit. Until the end of the turn your unit can shoot after Advancing or Falling Back, and its bolt pistols, boltguns, and combi-bolters gain the DEVASTATING WOUNDS ability while your unit has not already inflicted 6 wounds this turn using that ability. The key here is just that you can Advance or Fall Back and Shoot. But being able to Advance and Shoot is huge on Obliterators, who suffer from a 4" movement characteristic, or on bikes, where they can really stretch the field and still deliver some good bonus mortals, or on Havocs, who also like the extra movement. It's also pretty good on Bikers, who have high speed and a decent number of bolter shots to work with. It's less great on units that want to charge. That said, the DEVASTATING WOUNDS half of this has value on a unit of ten Terminators with combi-bolters, especially now that those are S5 AP-1 by default. Taking a unit with a Terminator Sorcerer in Cabal of Chaos and throwing out 36 S6 AP-1 bolter shots with full re-rolls to hit, LETHAL HITS, and DEVASTATING WOUNDS can be very nasty.
  • Let the Galaxy Burn (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – One non-TZEENTCH unit from your army that hasn’t shot yet gets [IGNORES COVER] on its ranged attacks and the attacks characteristic of torrent weapons in the unit becomes 6 until the end of your Shooting phase. They've carefully worded this to prevent you from taking it on Rubrics, but there's still plenty of value if you want to throw it on a unit of Plague Marines sporting four snot cannons. That said, the real value here is Ignores Cover, which is substantially better in 11th edition and great for making sure units of Terminators or Obliterators aren't losing shots to cover.
  • Millennia of Experience (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your opponent’s movement phase, after an enemy unit ends a Move within 8” of one of your INFANTRY or MOUNTED non-DAMNED units. You can immediately make a Normal move up to 6”. This is absolutely fantastic. Reactive moves are always great, and having one that gives you a full 6" move instead of D6 makes this reliably amazing. It's a great way for getting free movement to block enemies, deny charges and, most importantly, put a unit that's wholly within 9" of a transport back inside. Opponents always have to plan around this while you have 1 CP open and it's one of the most powerful effects in the game. That said, smart opponents will plan around it, so be careful not to over-extend. Your best value from something like this will always come from having two in your back pocket - having Huron in this Detachment gives you  a lot of options.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

Veterans of the Long War may not be the strongest detachment in Codex: Chaos Space Marines, but it’s still pretty good. That core ability is very strong and more importantly, it’s generically strong - there really aren't many units which won’t benefit from the Focus of Hatred ability. It's a Detachment built for Legionaries, Predators, Obliterators, and Vindicators, and those are all very strong units to build and play around. Being able to focus down big targets really helps shore up one of the bigger weaknesses of the Chaos Space Marines, which is that they lack some of the truly hard-hitting weapon options of their loyalist cousins. Additionally, mobility tricks like being able to fall back or advance and shoot via Stratagems gives units like Obliterators and Havocs a ton more utility, and being able to use Millennia of Experience to reactive move around key threats gives you a ton of counterplay, either to get away from threats, move block with key units, steal an objective, or get into position for a charge.

The biggest value in this Detachment comes out of the fact that it's only 2 DP, letting you pair it with one of the newer 1 DP options. Of those, the best is the Cabal of Chaos, which supercharges your PSYKER units and Daemon Princes. There the play is usually to take a Terminator Sorcerer with a unit of ten Terminators, letting you tag a unit with Death Hex for +1 AP and then blasting it full of holes with 36 S6 AP-2 bolter shots and another 8 Reaper Autocannons. Being able to do that after Advancing and adding DEVASTATING WOUNDS with the Black Crusade Stratagem. Your Terminators already guilt built-in re-rolls to hit, so you don't actually need the Detachment rule for them - that's generally why players opt for Warpstrike Champions when building around Cabal. But taking Warpstrike Champoins locks you into Disruption, and that Disposition sucks. You may not get uppy-downy here, but what you do get is the ability to use Focus of Hatred to supercharge your Chosen brick and Warp Talons. Your Chosen + Masters of the Maelstrom + Fabius Bile have both S6 AP-1 combi-bolters and S6 melee weapons and will get full re-rolls to hit from the Detachment Rule. That's solid!

Despite looking like a Black Legion detachment, this doesn’t really scream out for Abaddon. That said, there’s some real value here in being able to put Abaddon with a unit of Chosen and just rock his 4+ invulnerable aura all game and not have to worry about re-rolling hits. The downside here is that you really want Abaddon somewhere he can get re-rolls to wound so he can fish for Devastating Wounds with Drach’nyen, and not having that on offer here stinks. Abaddon + Masters + Chosen is also an OK option if you'd rather take him than Fabius Bile. Kravek Morne and his Mutilators also really like getting full re-rolls to hit.

Strengths

  • Versatility. Detachment ability works with pretty much any unit in the game, freeing you up to build however you want. It's always powerful and works well with your army's Dark Pacts ability.
  • Taking on Big Threats. Full re-rolls to hit against a key target is huge for taking out your opponent's most powerful unit early in the game to cripple them.
  • Reactive Movement. That reactive move is such a huge ability it's almost worth taking this Detachment just for it alone.

Weaknesses

  • Hordes. That Detachment ability isn't great against horde armies where re-rolls to hit aren't as necessary, and into something like a lot of War Dogs or Armigers you're really going to struggle.
  • Skill Requirement. This is a very skill-intensive detachment; knowing which threats to pick as a Focus of Hatred and how to use your units against them requires a ton of skill and there are easier detachments out there to use.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

A Sample List

As mentioned earlier, the big value here is combining Veterans with Cabal of Chaos to get really nasty Terminator and Chosen units. Trae Burnett took this list to a 4-1, 3rd place finish at the Denver Fight Club Gt in early October, 2026.

The core here is that 10-man unit of Terminators with the Sorcerer in Terminator Armour. This unit is one of the few that does want to take Eager for Vengeance, because the chances you'll get charged and want to fall back and shoot something are fairly large and getting a benefit to do it is a good thing. Kravek and his Mutiliators are the second big threat, and the Defiler is the third. The Cultists are sticky/action monkeys, while bikes make good fast, durable utility pieces and the Possessed Bricks will sneak up on players who aren't respecting them enough and going after the Defiler.

Final Thoughts

This is a tricky Detachment. The raw power here comes from re-rolls to hit, which makes a lot of otherwise high variance units like Vindicators and Obliterators much more powerful. But don't sleep on the movement tech - being able to disengage and re-engage from combat is huge, and that reactive move can do a ton of work. Chaos Space Marines already have good damage and output, so when you give them their own versions of the loyalists' fancy movement tricks, they get a huge boost.

title: MTG Commander banlist 2026
content:
Looking for the MTG Commander banlist? Commander is a vast, powerful, and ever-changing format, so it's crucial to stay on top of card bans. If you need a quick reminder of which cards can and can't go in your favorite deck, here's a complete list of Commander bans, from the latest to the very first.

So far, there have been 83 banned cards in MTG's Commander format. Use the links below to check out the latest changes and updates; the full banlist; or Wizards' new system of Game Changers and play brackets in EDH, explained. For more bans in other formats, see our full MTG banlist tracker.

  • Latest Commander banlist update
  • Full Commander banlist
  • Game Changers list
  • Brackets explained

Latest Commander banlist update

On February 9, 2026, Wizards of the Coast unbanned two Commander cards:

  • Biorhythm
  • Lutri, the Spellchaser (except as Companion)

Lutri's case is obvious - it was only banned because it could serve as a Companion in any deck.

The decision to make a new designation 'banned as Companion' appeared to weigh heavily on the designers, based on Gavin Verhey's article - adding sub-lists increases complexity and the chance that players will bring a card in a slot it's not supposed to. The decision was deemed acceptable because the worst case scenario for player mistakes isn't that bad - you tell the player with Lutri in the companion slot that he's banned, and they drop him into the 99.

Because Lutri was banned for reasons not really related to power he bypassed the gamechangers list, where unbanned cards typically go.

Meanwhile, Biorhythm was unbanned following a trend of unbanning expensive, high-impact cards that have a big impact on the game. If Worldfire and Coalition Victory can be legal cards without messing up the format too much, so can Biorhythm.

Full Commander banlist

(8 of) The Power 9

  • Ancestral Recall - banned April 2005
  • Black Lotus - banned April 2005
  • Mox Emerald - banned April 2005
  • Mox Jet - banned April 2005

  • Mox Sapphire - banned April 2005
  • Time Walk - banned April 2005

It's no surprise to see these here. If any card was going to be banned in Commander, it would be the Power 9 - some of the most broken cards ever made in Magic, each offering absurd value for their mana cost.

Speaking of cost, what's interesting is that it was their price point, not their power level, that originally saw these cards consigned to the Commander banlist - in the very first spate of bannings back in 2005.

The RC was worried that these cards would auto-includes for anyone wanting a really strong deck, and didn't want the fan-made format to have a perceived budget of thousands of dollars.

You might notice only 8/9ths of the Power 9 is actually banned. Timetwister is really an honorary member of the gang - it's busted when played with cards from the other 8. But in fact, a wheel, even a really great wheel like Timetwister, isn't worth making a fuss about.

Nine cards that reference 'playing for ante' are banned in Commander and all other formats. This is because they don't work within the rules. Playing for keeps in a four-player game is probably a bad bet anyhow. The banned MTG ante cards are:

Game Changers list

In 2025, Wizards of the Coast introduced a separate but linked 'Game Changers' list to the banlist conversation. Game Changers are cards that dramatically warp a game when (or shortly after) they're played. The number of game changers a deck contains is one factor in determining which Commander 'bracket' it falls into during pre-game discussions.

Though certainly not banned - or even at risk of banning - Wizards has made it clear that future banned cards are likely to come from this list. Similarly, any cards that get unbanned are likely to move onto the Game Changers list.

Brackets explained

The beta brackets system is a tool to help Commander players talk about the gameplay experience they want to create with their deck. Each bracket has a set of deck-building conditions: if a deck meets those conditions, it sits in that bracket.

1. Exhibition

Decks prioritize theme over function and showcase a unique idea or experience over valuing winning.

  • No game changers
  • No mass land denial
  • No extra turns
  • No two-card infinite combos (game-enders, lockouts, or infinite)
  • Few tutors

2. Core

Decks are focused, even if every card choice isn't the highest power, and comparable to an average precon. Wins are often telegraphed or incremental.

  • No game changers
  • No mass land denial
  • No chaining extra turns
  • No two-card infinite combos (game-enders, lockouts, or infinite)
  • Few tutors

3. Upgraded

Decks are thoughtfully designed, full of synergistic or strong cards. Games could end out of nowhere with powerful spells and late-game combos.

  • No mass land denial
  • No chaining extra turns
  • Late game, two-card infinite combos allowed
  • Up to three game changers

4. Optimized

Decks are turbocharged with the most powerful cards in the format. Everybody intends to win and is ready to play against anything.

No restrictions other than the banlist.

5. CEDH

Decks are built to win in the competitive metagame. Players intend to use only the most powerful strategies.

  • No restrictions other than the banlist.

Are Commander brackets power levels?

Commander brackets are numbered, but these numbers don't measure the power level of a deck. The higher the bracket, the more tools the deck has to succeed in competitive, meta-focused gameplay. The lower the bracket, the more casual and focused on 'doing something neat with friends' the deck is.

Hopefully, players can use the brackets to choose decks that have similar gameplay goals. There will still be decks that perform well above or below what their bracket suggests.

You'll find a welcoming community in the free Wargamer Discord who are eager to discuss your latest deck brews with you. To make sure you don't miss the best stories on Wargamer each week, sign up to our newsletter.

title: Pokémon's best rival has a new brand new card, but only in China
content:
The Pokémon TCG has just announced three full art Pokémon cards which will be exclusively available in China, and be prepared to get jealous, because there's a brand new N card among them.

Two of these cards, N's Plan and Hilda, are appearing in the Chinese version of Black Bolt and White Flare, which launches November 6 this year. We've got a fierce looking Hilda here, and an N with the blue lights of a city behind him.

The English version of N's Plan remains one of the most sought after cards in Black Bolt, though perhaps not as pricey as some fans thought it would be for one of the most popular Pokémon characters of all time - generally going for about $50-60. In my view, this one's significantly better, though your mileage may vary. It's maybe not as pretty as the original, but I like the colors and the composition more.

Alongside the Chinese Blaze Black/White Flare release is Gem Pack 7, the country's miniature booster packs that have only four cards apiece - with lots of different stamps and foil treatments. The selling point for this one, however, is an SAR version of Misty's Psyduck.

The original Misty's Psyduck SAR was beautiful, but this one is almost too cute. It features Psyduck chilling on a deckchair with a beachball, while its trainer walks up the beach to greet him. It's bound to be a sought after card for Psyduck fans and Misty fans alike - basically anyone who loves Gen 1.

Unfortunately for everyone else, historically these China-only cards have remained region-locked; it's unlikely they'll be printed in English, at least not any time soon. If you don't mind not being able to read them, you can still buy these cards on the secondary market, but it won't be cheap. Some (like the Gengar Pikachu, priced around $2,000) are among the most expensive Pokémon cards of the modern day.

As its TCG releases rapidly catch up with the baseline, China seems to be getting a rather large proportion of exclusive content. Regularly, the region gets its own unique cards, but I was particularly envious of the 30th anniversary Charizard figurine from a couple months back.

title: [40K] Weekend Update: October 19, 2026
content:
In our Weekend update series, we cover the big events and stories that are happening each week in wargames, so you can stay updated and informed every week. The 40k side will be mostly covered by me, Isaac Terada, while Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson covers the non-40k side of event coverage and news. 

Mid-size Singles Events Dominate the Weekend as Paris Wargames Expo Finishes Today

After a slow weekend last week, singles events for Warhammer 40k had a return to form this week with six events boasting more than 70 players. The biggest event of the weekend was the Paris Wargame Expo 2, a 40k singles event with 212 players, marking it as a proper major. As of this writing the event is still ongoing, and will conclude today. It’s currently difficult to tell which players are in the event’s top cut (8 players), as the results do not appear to be displaying correctly in Best coats Pairings It appears that the event’s top 8 includes a surprising number of Necrons players, along with Leagues of Votann, Dark Angels, Astra Militarum, and Death Guard.

UPDATE: The Top 8

We have the top 8 available:

Quarterfinals

  • Arnaud (92) v Clément (78)
  • Marin (100) v Hugo (25)
  • Alban (100) v José (25)
  • Léo (78) v Quentin (85)

Semifinals

  • Marin v Arnaud
  • Alban v Quentin

Damien Cooper Wins the Alba GT with Orks

Moving on to events which actually completed, Damien Cooper won the 2026 Alba GT in Székesfehérvár, Hungary - the weekend’s second largest event, with 99 players. Damien scored a perfect 500 battle points over the weekend running an Orks list running Reconnaissance with Brute Bosses, Bully Boyz, and Da Big Hunt. There were four other undefeated players at the five round event. Damien has been running Orks since May after switch from Death Guard and placed third with Orks at the Leoben Autumn Spring event in late September. He’s currently 186th in the ITC with this event.

Ben Greenlay Takes Gold with Grey Knights at Bloodshed Bay

Ben Greenlay won the weekend’s third largest event - Bloodshed Bay Two, a 77-player singles event held in Ontario over the weekend, defeating Marco Zecconi’s Orks in the final round en route to a 589/600 score for the event. Ben’s Warpbane Task Force list, which he ran with Purge the Foe as his Disposition, featured two Grand Master Nemesis Dreadknights, a single unit of five Terminators with a Grandmaster, a pair of Razorbacks, and an Eversor Assassin. Ben’s win at the event moves him to 101st in the ITC global rankings.

Matt Bell Wins the That 6++ Grand Tournament: South

Matt Bell took home gold at the 74-player That 6++ GT over the weekend, winning the weekend’s fourth largest event with his Necrons (Skyshroud Spearhead + Cursed Legion).

Another Killer Teams Weekend

It was a big weekend for teams events as two countries ran their national team championship events. The largest of these was the Italian teams national championship, a six-man teams event held in Italy, followed by the five-man Scottish Open Championship (won by Stat Check), and the 8-man Tennessee Elite Open (won by the Warp Dust Crusaders).

Altrimenti ci Arrabbiamo Win the Italian Team National Championships

Altrimenti ci Arrabbiamo (which loosely translates to something like “Alternatively, we’ll get angry”) won the largest teams event of the weekend - the 2026 Italian Team National Championship, featuring 264 players competing over five rounds with teams of six. Congratulations to Andrea Manfroni, Francesco Di Bonaventura, Ludovico Mazza, Nicolo Gili, Pietro Riccio, and Simone Caroselli for winning the event with a 5-0 record.

Stat Check Wins the Scottish Open Team Championship

Stat Check took an absolutely loaded team to the 140-player event this year, and Innes Wilson, Liam Vsl, Nathan RobertsGustavo José Branco Varandas de Sousa, Maciej ‘Pumba’ Guziec, and Nassim Fouchane took gold at the event with a 100-0 win in the final round over Black Crow Gaming. Ironically the team’s toughest matchup was in round 4 against team “Stat Check Uncs,” featuring a number of their teammates.

Deathwatch Terminators by Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

OH GOD DEATHWATCH OH MY GOD

Codex Marines is officially here, and some of its biggest problems have become clear. Deathwatch-flavored Marines (armies with Deathwatch Detachments) put up a staggering 69% true win rate this weekend, capturing 8% of all TiWP (Tournament in Winning Position) spots. Comparatively, the next highest results were for the Adeptus Mechanicus, whose true win % was only 55%.

It’s clear that the Deathwatch are a problem in the current meta; Marine armies without Deathwatch support posted only a 42% win rate over the weekend, though this is in part due to the game’s best players opting to run Deathwatch as the obvious best choice from a Codex packed with solid options. Among non-Deathwatch Marine armies, Space Wolves appear to be the best flavor, as the speedy, melee-heavy army loves the Assault Brethren and Terminator Storm Force Detachments.

Beyond the overall dominance of Deathwatch, we saw a surprisingly good spread of even winners this weekend, with standout showings from Tyranids, Necrons, and Grey Knights, each of which had two event wins. They were joined by the Adeptus Mechanicus and World Eaters, the latter of which boasted the weekend’s best Event Results as the changes to Berzerker Warband opened things up for the faction.

The Death Guard also saw a large jump in the results this weekend with four players achieving TiWP results, primarily on the back of Shamblerot + Paragons lists. Keep an eye on them and World Eaters next week - there may be a new build coming for them from Innes or Folger.

The Grand Narrative Announces Its Lords of War 

Games Workshop announced four of the Lords of War for their annual Grand Narrative Event this weekend, showcasing what appears to be two of the Lords of War for Chaos and two for the Imperium faction. This year’s event looks to take place in the Maelstrom, where players will be fighting over the planet of Ferrum’s Wake, a world currently under the iron-fisted rule of Kaelen Voss, a former Red Corsair who preaches a kind of radical anarchy. He’s currently being hunted by both the Imperium and Huron’s own forces.

Player Focus: Folger Pyles

Folger is one of the players that everyone knows. In comparison to some of the other top threats he is much newer to the game but he has left an impact. Winning the ITC last year and grabbing first at Warmasters and WTC this year he is one of the most acclaimed players of the modern 40k era. He hasn’t pushed quite as hard at ITC this year, only currently ranking in at 26th, probably pushing him out of this year's winning position, but with a good enough WCW run he may have a shot. He is pushing up his rankings in other places however with a 6th on Stat Check elo’s ranking, where he has been holding in to the top for a long time.

Folger is not quite a faction expert but not quite a faction hopper. He tends to stick with a faction for a pretty long time even when afterward he moves to a different one. He became basically the faction spokesman for Adeptus Custodes for a year, but before then he was an Aeldari specialist, and now just this weekend he is taking a crack with Death Guard. Maybe we can convince him to bring Agents to WCW if we ask hard enough.

Alongside our coverage of the what's-what of 40k each week, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson joins us to provide some quick updates on the movers and shakers in the competitive scene of some of the other games we cover here at Tabletop Battles!

Tomb Kings on the Horizon for Old World

This week’s Sunday preview takes us to the shifting sands of the Old World, as the Sunday preview over on Warhammer Community revealed that the Tomb Kings are next on the release docket. This second wave of Tomb Kings includes new Skeleton Warrior, Skeleton Archer, and Skeleton Chariot kits, first available in the Host of Nehekhara Army Reinforcement Set. Alongside this release will see a new Arcane Journal for Tomb Kings, The River of Bones, which expands upon both the Tomb Kings and Wood Elves factions, including Armies of Infamy for both factions.

Oh, also a new Red Gobbo is going on preorder this week, and he has a little sled new, which is cute and fun. Glad the Red Gobbo is just out here having a grand ol’ time.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Two European Events Dominate Age of Sigmar Headlines

While there were multiple reasonably large events this weekend for Age of Sigmar, such as the Through the Breach invitational in Canada and the Sparkle Party Death Match in Seattle, the European scene made the biggest splash in the Sigmar world this weekend with both the Paris Expo in France and Trials GX in Italy.

The Paris Expo event was a singles event that consisted of 83 players, with five rounds played between Saturday and Sunday. Two players emerged with undefeated records, with battle points as the tie breaker. In second place we have Tristan Darde with Sylvaneth, piloting a list consisting of Allarielle, Drycha, Belthanos, and a Spirit of Druthu with some Dryads and a Warsong Revenant to support. In first place undefeated we go from rampant life to rampant undeath with Nicolas Eisenberg’s Soulblight Gravelords. Nicolas’s Soulblight list was just as big on the big monsters as Tristan’s was, bringing Prince Vhordrai, Lauka Vai, Radukar the Beast, and a Vengorian Lord, supported by three units of the Warcry monster hunter vampires, the Askurgan Trueblades. Congratulations to both Tristan and Nicolas for their outstanding performances here!

Even larger than the Paris Expo though was the Trials GX 2026 event held in Italy, a massive teams event consisting of 193 players. The teams format has been on a hot streak in Age of Sigmar over the past few weeks, and this event certainly takes the cake as far as the sheer scope of players involved. The event consisted of teams of six players competing over five rounds, with only one team going undefeated over the course of the weekend. That team, Flamingo Weapon, consisted of players piloting Soulblight, Nighthaunt, Hedonism, Ogors, Daughters of Khaine, and Sylvaneth. Another huge congratulations to Flamingo Weapon’s team members for the huge showing at such a massive event!

SPIEL Essen Kicks off this Week

One of the largest tabletop gaming expos in the world, Germany’s SPIEL Essen event, kicks off this week and promises to bring not only a huge wave of reveals and games from across the gaming space, but the convention is the current home of Europe’s Golden Daemon challenge.

The convention attracts over 200,000 attendees internationally across over 1,000 vendors, and will run from October 22nd to October 25th. The weekend consists of vendor booths, organized and casual play, panels, and hobby classes for attendees to partake in. Golden Daemon, which moved its home to SPIEL last year, is one of the biggest draws at the event, with hobbyists competing across a multitude of categories to create stunning miniatures of the highest level for a chance to win the coveted Slayer Sword award.

We will be sure to update here next week with some of the big reveals from this marquee event, as well as the winners from Golden Daemon.

Fliers Are Swooping in to Star Wars: Legion

One of Star Wars’s most iconic bits are the starfighters, with ships like the X-Wing and TIE Fighter speeding and soaring through the imagination of folks for fifty years. Now, Star Wars fans can bring these famous craft to tabletops near them, as Fliers were announced late last week for Star Wars: Legion.

This first wave of craft, set to launch in February of next year, will allow players to use these airborne predators as support for their ground forces during games of Legion, and currently one ship is planned for each of Legion’s four factions. These ships include X-wings, TIE fighters, Vulture Droids, V-Wings, and Fang Fighters, with additional fighters possible in the future.

No rules have been revealed yet, but the AMG team was eager to talk about bringing these flyers into the game in the announcement video, giving us a taste of what we can potentially expect when they release in full next year. Until then, we will have to wait patiently for more news and keep a sharp eye for any other teasers AMG might offer.

title: Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha from Freecompany
content:
Freecompany, the group behind Eldfall Chronicles, has recently announced a new entry in their line of dungeon crawl releases. Like their previous Northern Wind dungeon crawl, Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha will be a cooperative game allowing 1-4 players to journey through a campaign story that boasts multiple branching storylines. Follow its progress over on Gamefound and get ready to back it when it goes live on November 10!

Apocrypha

Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha is set three years after the conclusion of the Northern Wind expedition (see our review from last year). This time, instead of traveling up a windblown and snowy mountain, the heroes are venturing into the Grand Library located in the Sand Kingdoms. There, they will explore the Sealed Archives to uncover lost knowledge, face eldritch threats, and hunt for the profane tomes known as the Apocrypha.

Continuing the trend of all of the Eldfall Chronicles releases, Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha is fully compatible with their other dungeon crawl games as well as skirmish wargame mode of playing.

So far a handful of the monsters within the library have been showcased as well as the four main heroes that will be attempting to solve the mysteries within the Grand Library. Each of the four main factions of the skirmish game are represented here: Ferron from the Helian League, Rien of the Coalition of Thenion, Kimiko from the Empire of Soga, and Cyrus of the Sand Kingdoms.

title: All official DnD races and species explained
content:
DnD races represent the different species found in the world's oldest tabletop RPG. Your DnD species (as they've been recently re-named) decides your appearance and culture, but it also determines rules-relevant facts about your size, speed, and abilities.

There are dozens upon dozens of official Dungeons and Dragons races, though the current Player's Handbook features just 10. Whether you want to play a standard species or something rarer, your choice has a big impact on your character. I've painstakingly researched each possible option and explained how they work in this guide.

Before you start shopping for a new species, a few housekeeping rules. D&D 5e now has its own refreshed sub-edition, 5.5e. Some species appear in both, but others don't. I've made it clear where you can find the most up-to-date version of each option. For brevity's sake, I've also only presented the most recent rules - though I've listed other, older sourcebooks you can investigate yourself if you prefer 2014 to 2024.

Also, this isn't my only guide to character creation. I recommend checking out Wargamer's guides to DnD classes and DnD backgrounds, as they complement the character options here pretty well! Okay, now we're ready to begin:

The core DnD races are:

  • Aasimar
  • Dragonborn
  • Dwarf
  • Elf
  • Gnome
  • Goliath
  • Halfling
  • Half-Elf
  • Half-Orc
  • Human
  • Orc
  • Tiefling

The rarer DnD races include:

  • Aarakocra
  • Astral Elf
  • Autognome
  • Bugbear
  • Boggart
  • Centaur
  • Changeling
  • Deep Gnome

Aasimar

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forCleric, Warlock, Paladin
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

Thanks to a shared ancestry with celestials, each Aasimar is blessed with divine looks and abilities. They're naturally resistant to necrotic and radiant damage, plus they're gifted healers who can roll d4s equal to their proficiency bonus to restore a creature's HP.

All Aasimar can cast the Light cantrip using Charisma as their spellcasting modifier, which implies the optimal builds for this species rely on that stat. However, if you're happy to sacrifice this (very situational) cantrip, an Aasimar can excel in any D&D class.

The Aasimar's most explosive feature is Celestial Revelation. When activated, this can give your Aasimar a fly speed, create a ten-foot emanation of light that deals radiant damage, or force enemies to make a Charisma save or become frightened. Whichever form they take, it lets the Aasimar deal additional radiant or necrotic damage when they attack.

Learn more in our full Aasimar species guide.

Dragonborn

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Strength, +1 Charisma (2014 rules only)
Best forPaladin, Barbarian, Warlock
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Dragonborn resemble humanoid dragons, though D&D lore flip-flops on exactly how this species got its draconic features. However it happened, the Dragonborn's scaly, wingless appearance makes them one of the most recognizable species.

Their signature Breath Weapon helps in that department, too. Able to exhale a force of destructive energy that deals 1d10 damage on a failed Constitution saving throw, they've got an ace in the hole straight out of the gate. Its damage and difficulty class will increase as they level up, and your choice of Draconic Ancestry will determine its damage type, as well as your character's damage resistances.

The Dragonborn also benefits from 60 feet of Darkvision. More excitingly, once they reach level five, they can grow wings as a bonus action to gain a fly speed. We'd recommend this species for martials that usually lack ranged options and mobility.

Learn more in our DnD Dragonborn species guide.

Dwarf

SizeMedium
Speed25ft (2014) or 30ft (2024)
Ability scores+2 Constitution (2014 rules only)
Best forCleric, Fighter, Barbarian, Druid
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Originally members of cave-dwelling clans, the DnD Dwarf species has a reputation for durability and a handy way with stone. Mechanically, this manifests as a resistance to poison damage and advantage on saving throws against being poisoned.

Dwarfs also have the Dwarven Toughness feature, which automatically increases their maximum hit points by one, and it does so again with every DnD level up. It doesn't get much more durable than that. Unsurprisingly, the classes that tend to suit a Dwarf are those looking to keep themselves standing on the front lines of battle.

Beyond this, a Dwarf's skills are defined by their ancient tendency to yearn for the mines. They have extended Darkvision (120ft rather than the standard 60ft) and tremorsense for 60 feet instead of enhanced History rolls when checking out pieces of rock - far more useful, if you ask us.

Learn more in our complete DnD Dwarf guide.

Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Dexterity (2014 rules only)
Best forRogue, Ranger, Wizard, Warlock
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Tall, sleek, and pointy-eared, The DnD Elf is a graceful being, most at home in ethereal forests. Their Darkvision and proficiency in either Insight, Perception, or Survival make them excellent stealthy scouts. Elves also have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and they enter trances instead of going to sleep at night.

Each Elf has an Elven Lineage that decides some of their natural abilities. This makes the Elf an immensely flexible species, perfect for many kinds of characters (though, most of the time, we tend to recommend it for spellcasters).

Drow have enhanced Darkvision, and they can cast Dancing Lights, Faerie Fire, and Darkness. High Elves know Prestidigitation, Detect Magic, and Misty Step - though they can swap the cantrip with another from the Wizard spell list each day. Wood Elves have a base speed of 35 feet, as well as the ability to cast Druidcraft, Longstrider, and Pass Without Trace.

Learn more in our DnD Elf species guide.

Gnome

SizeSmall
Speed25ft (2014) or 30 feet (2024)
Ability scores+2 Intelligence (2014 rules only)
Best forWizard, Rogue, Artificer
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Vibrant and expressive, DnD Gnomes are often styled as a curious and cunning race that enjoys the thrill of adventure. However you choose to roleplay them, all Gnomes gain the same basic benefits - Darkvision, plus advantage on all Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws.

When you decide to play a Gnome, you'll choose a specific Gnomish Lineage. Forest Gnomes are illusionists who can speak to small beasts (often without wasting a spell slot). Meanwhile, Rock Gnomes can cast Mending and Prestidigitation, and they can still tinker with tools to create a small mechanical device.

A species that gains extra spells is usually a surefire pick for a spellcasting class, as it beefs up their existing repertoire. The Rogue is our wildcard suggestion, though. Gnomes are great at finding non-violent solutions to problems, which pairs well with the Rogue's utility-focused approach.

Learn more about this species in our DnD Gnome guide.

Goliath

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet (2014) or 35 feet (2024)
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

A DnD Goliath may only be slightly bigger than your average human, but they have strength that rivals their Giant ancestors. They're as durable as granite, and they make for great martial characters.

The Goliath has advantage on checks against the grappled condition, and from level five onwards, they can become Large for 10 minutes, which gives them advantage on Strength checks and increases their speed by 10 feet, as well as greatly enlarging the area they affect in combat. Hulk, smash!

Additionally, the Goliath chooses one ability that's unique to their Giant Ancestry. This might allow them to teleport as a bonus action, deal extra damage, slow or knock enemies prone, or even reduce the damage the Goliath takes. Giant Ancestry is so versatile that you could play six or seven Goliaths and not have one feel same-y.

Learn more in our DnD Goliath guide.

Halfling

SizeSmall
Speed25ft (2014) or 30ft (2024)
Ability scores+2 Dexterity (2014 rules only)
Best forRogue, Ranger, Bard
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Halflings are almost identical to the Hobbits of Tolkien's Middle-earth, though without the thick foot hair and round front doors. Living in peaceful, bucolic communities usually hidden from the conflicts of the world, they're cheerful and curious.

Halflings are extra nimble, able to move through the space of any creature that's at least one DnD size larger than them. They're also brave, with advantage on saves against the frightened condition, and lucky, meaning they're able to reroll any 1 on a d20. As well as luck and courage, Halflings have stealth to fall back on, as they can Hide as long as they're obscured by a creature at least one size larger than them.

All kinds of characters benefit from extra luck, but we tend to build Halfling characters that get maximum value from their stealth and mobility. That means Scout characters and anyone who needs an easy way to escape mid-fight.

For a full description, check out our DnD Halfling guide.

Half-Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 any other stat (2014 rules only)
Best forBard, Sorcerer
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2014)

Born of Human and Elf parents, DnDHalf-Elf characters take bits from both of their ancestral lines. Thanks to their Elf lineage, they have Darkvision and are immune to being put to sleep. They also have the versatility of Humans, which gives them proficiency in two extra DnD skills.

Like Elves, Half-Elves have a subrace that can give them further powers. However, if you want to take the optional features of a Drow, High, or Wood Half-Elf, you must sacrifice the extra skill proficiencies granted by your Human ancestry. In their place, you can learn additional spells, become trained in additional weapons, or gain a swimming speed.

Species of dual parentage like the Half-Elf and the Half-Orc (who we'll discuss in a moment) weren't included in the 2024 Player's Handbook, so you'll only have the 2014 version to work with. Still, their flexible DnD stats and skills make them strong Charisma casters. The Bard is our top choice of class for the species overall.

Want to learn more? Here's our full DnD Half-Elf species guide.

Half-Orc

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Strength, +1 Constitution (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2014)

With Orc and Human blood running through their veins, Half-Orcs partially resemble the classic Tolkien-esque creatures. They're physically mighty, and they may have visible teeth and green-ish skin.

Their famed physical might is realized through their Relentless Endurance and Savage Attacks. The first ability means that, should a Half-Orc be downed in battle, they can immediately bounce back with one HP. Savage Attack, meanwhile, lets them roll an additional attack die whenever they land a critical hit - perfect for massive bursts of damage.

Like the Half-Elf, the Half-Orc was left out of the 2024 rules update. However, you can still shoehorn them into your games thanks to backwards compatibility. Whether you use their associated ability score increase or not, Half-Orcs are best suited to melee-based martial classes.

Here's a complete guide to the DnD Half-Orc that can tell you more.

Human

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 in all stats, or +1 in two stats plus a feat and skill (2014 rules only)
Best forAll
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

DnD Human characters are variable and adaptable folks, who ambitiously explore the land for both personal gain and altruistic devotion. Their lives are short, but their empires are enormous.

Humans are by far the most versatile of the common species. The 2014 version gives you complete control over your ability score increases, and the popular Variant Human gains a feat for free straight out of the gate.

In the 2024 rules, every character gains a free DnD 2024 feat at level one, but the Human can choose a second feat. They also start with an extra skill proficiency, and they gain Inspiration whenever they finish a long rest. Whichever version of the Human you're planning to use, they're an excellent choice for basically any class.

Learn more in our DnD Human species guide.

Orc

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two stats or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forPaladin, Cleric, Fighter
SourcebookPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Eberron: Rising from the Last War (2019)

While they're stereotyped as villains in a lot of fantasy media (including past editions of D&D), the Orc 5e has as much right to be a heroic adventurer as anyone else. The Half-Orc's large teeth, green skin, and physical might are all inherited from this species.

An Orc is best known for their imposing strength. Like the Half-Orc, this is represented by the Relentless Endurance ability, which lets them drop to one hit point instead of zero if they are downed in combat. Additionally, Adrenaline Rush lets them dash as a bonus action, Rogue-style, and it gives the Orc temporary HP equal to their proficiency bonus.

Orcs are a natural choice for Strength-based martial builds, though always going for Strength-based builds might start to feel a bit same-y after a while. If you want to shake it up, any fragile spellcaster would appreciate abilities that help them to avoid death.

Tiefling

SizeMedium or Small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 Intelligence (2014 rules only)
Best forWarlock, Sorcerer, Wizard
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes (2018); Player's Handbook (2014)

Tieflings have a unique appearance, thanks to their horns, tails, and vibrantly colored skin. These traits come from their ancestry, as somewhere along the line a devil, demon, or yugoloth joined or afflicted their family. This heritage also provides them with resistance to certain DnD damage types and extra spellcasting abilities.

While there are a vast number of Tiefling variants in D&D's many books, the 2024 variant of 5e presents three. Abyssal Tieflings are resistant to poison damage, and they learn Poison Spray, Ray of Sickness, and Hold Person. Chthonic Tieflings are resistant to necrotic damage, and they learn Chill Touch, False Life, and Ray of Enfeeblement. Finally, Infernal Tieflings have fire resistance, and they'll learn Fire Bolt, Hellish Rebuke, and Darkness.

Learn more in our Tiefling 5e and DnD 2024 Tiefling guides.

Aarakocra

SizeMedium
Speed25ft (walking); 50ft (flying while not wearing medium or heavy armor)
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Rogue, Fighter
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Elemental Evil Player's Companion (2015)

The standout feature of the bird-like Aarakocra is their flight. With a large pair of feathered wings sprouting from their back, they were the first playable D&D race that could fly, letting them soar above enemies to pick them off from afar. They have a natural +2 Dexterity and +1 Wisdom increase, and they also sport a pair of talons that let you deal damage equal to 1d4 + your Strength modifier.

Given their natural Dex increase, an Aaarakocra can make a brilliant DnD Ranger, especially if paired with the Archery fighting style to make use of their mobility. The DnD Rogue is also a good choice, as Flight lets you hop about hiding places with even more ease. If you want a more martial build, go for a DnD Fighter specializing in Finesse weapons. Flight will help you traverse the battlefield.

For a full run-through of the best Aarakocra names, classes, and builds, check out our full Aarakocra 5e species guide.

Astral Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forBard
SourcebooksSpelljammer: Adventures in Space (2022)

The Astral Elf 5e comes from literal, actual space (or the Astral Plane, as D&D calls it). They have many of the standard Elf's abilities, including Darkvision, advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and the ability to go into a trance rather than sleep. Starlight Step also lets them teleport 30 feet as a bonus action, and they're naturally proficient in Perception.

The Astral Trance is a bit different from the respite that other Elves get. Whenever you finish a trance, you gain proficiency with one skill and weapon/tool from the Player's Handbook. You can switch these every time you take a DnD long rest - perfect for the party Skill Monkey. 

Autognome

SizeSmall
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAll
SourcebooksSpelljammer: Adventures in Space (2022)

The fifth edition Spelljammer books gave us the Autognome 5e, and these pint-sized automatons are suitable for pretty much any class.

Their metal bodies give them a base armor class of 13 + your Dexterity modifier, even without armor. That's handy for anyone who isn't relying on Strength or heavy armor to protect them. Plus, the excellent 'Built for Success' ability lets you add 1d4 to any attack roll, ability check, or saving throw you make, and you can do so multiple times per day.

The Autognome's remaining abilities are a bit situational - the ability to spend Hit Dice when someone casts mending on you, plus two extra tool proficiencies and the ability to remain conscious while resting. However, this species remains an unusual yet competent all-rounder.

Bugbear

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three
Best forBarbarian, Monk, Warlock
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

Once one of the most recognizable DnD monsters, members of the Bugbear 5e race are also available as player-character options. They're the hairy, stocky cousins of goblins, and they have a little bit of Feywild magic to help them with skills like stealth.

As well as being proficient in stealth, Bugbears can deal a Surprise Attack (and an extra 2d6 damage) to any creature that hasn't taken a turn yet in combat. While a Rogue might seem like an obvious choice for a Bugbear, that Surprise Attack is useful for pretty much any class in battle. Bugbears also have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, but that's less relevant to choosing the right class for your build.

For full details on how you can become a big ol' Bugbear, check out our complete Bugbear 5e species guide.

Boggart

SizeSmall
Speed30 feet
Ability scores-
Best forFighter, Ranger, Paladin, Sorcerer, Warlock
SourcebooksLorwyn: First Light (2025)

Hailing from the MTG plane of Lorwny/Shadowmoor, the Boggart is a kind of crafty goblinoid. Their appearances can be hugely varied, from hedgehog-like to horned and furry.

All Boggarts, however, come with 60 feet of Darkvision, plus the Fey's classic advantage against being charmed. Your more unique traits are 'Nimble Escape' and 'Fury of the Small'. The first lets you Disengage or Hide as a bonus action, while the second lets you deal extra damage equal to your proficiency bonus when you hit a creature larger than you. This is a solid hit-and-run species that appeals to martial characters, but blasters and gishes can have plenty of fun too.

Centuar

Size40ft
SpeedMedium
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Guildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

These half-humanoid, half-horse Fey creatures have an affinity with nature - and a powerful hind kick. As a Centaur 5e, you'll often be charging into battle - meaning that you'll move 30ft into melee range, hit with your weapons, and then get a Hooves attack with your bonus action. Your hooves are pretty hefty, dealing 1d6 plus your Strength modifier as an unarmed attack.

Centaurs can also choose to have proficiency in Animal Handling, Nature, Medicine, or Survival thanks to their Fey ties. They've got a superior carrying capacity to other creatures of their size, but please don't ask them to climb anything. The hooves make it very difficult. The hooves also limit your optimal class choices - you're best off playing frontline martial classes.

Changeling

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRogue, Bard
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Eberron: Rising from the Last War (2019); Eberron: Forge of the Artificer (2026)

A Changeling 5e has the power to completely alter their appearance as an action. Their ancestry essentially means that they have constant access to the Disguise Self spell, only with guaranteed success. As you can imagine, this means that Changelings excel in social situations - and sneaky subterfuge.

When you create a Changeling character, you can choose two extra skill proficiencies from Deception, Insight, Intimidation, or Persuasion. These additional Charisma-based skills, combined with that powerful shapeshifting ability, make the Changeling ideal for two character types in particular: the sneaky Rogue and the performative Bard.

Deep Gnome

SizeSmall
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Rogue
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Elemental Evil Player's Companion (2015)

Technically, the Deep Gnome 5e is a subrace of the regular Gnome species. However, depending on which books you're reading, you can also find complete rules for a separate Deep Gnome species. Whichever mechanics you plan to use, the basic concept is the same - these are Gnomes born in and shaped by the Underdark.

These Gnomes are tricksy, so their natural ability to cast Disguise Self and Nondetection come in handy. Similarly, they'll get great use out of the Svirfneblin Camouflage feature, which gives them advantage on Stealth checks a certain number of times per long rest. Lastly, your Deep Gnome will be naturally resistant to magic, so they have advantage on Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws against spells.

The Deep Gnome's features complement almost any class in D&D. We'd recommend playing whichever strikes your fancy - though, if you're looking to optimize at every possible turn, the Ranger and the Rogue get the most from the Svirfneblin mix of stealth and sorcery.

Dhampir

SizeMedium or small
Speed35ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Ranger, Monk
SourcebooksRavenloft: The Horrors Within (2026)

A Dhampir is a humanoid of another species that's reached a state of undeath most commonly associated with vampires. Perhaps one of those monsters transformed your Dhampir, or maybe they inherited the curse in some other dark way. Either way, they're almost unrecognizable in their new, undead form.

Your new features include 60 feet of Darkvision, a climbing speed equal to your walking speed (which you can use hands free from level 3 onwards!), and a tasty Vampiric Bite that lets you deal damage and regain HP with your fangs. Plus, the Trace of Undeath means you have Resistance to Necrotic damage.

The original version of the Dhampir from 2021's 'Van Richten's Guide to Ravenloft' was a 'lineage', a modified version of another race. It kept their skill proficiencies and unusual speed types (flying, climbing, etc.), but all other rules were replaced with that of a Dhampir. And unlike the 2026 Dhampir, it didn't need to breathe!

Learn more in our Dhampir 5e guide.

Duergar

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Paladin
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Sword Coast Adventurer's Guide (2015)

Originally a Dwarf subrace, the Duergar 5e became a separate species in Monsters of the Multiverse. Their rules are slightly different in this book, but they're still an Underdark species that shares many traits with its surface-dwelling cousins.

Duergar still have Dwarven Resilience, which gives them resistance to poison damage and advantage on saving throws against poison. They also still have 120ft of Darkvision and the ability to cast Invisibility and Enlarge/Reduce using their Duergar Magic.

The Duergar's sunlight sensitivity is (thankfully) gone, so they're not disadvantaged when adventuring during the day. They also have advantage on saving throws against being charmed or stunned. While flexible stats mean a Duergar is playable for pretty much any class, those that use magic to enhance their combat and stealth skills will maximize the Duergar's potential.

Duskling

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores-
Best forRogue, Bard, Sorcerer, Warlock
SourcebooksD&DBeyond Drops (2026)

Dusklings are Fey who have abandoned the Feywild for adventure further afield. You can find plenty of them on the material plane, but some migrate even further to the Outer Planes. Wherever they go, though, they maintain some of that tricksy Fey magic.

This manifests as 60 feet of Darkvision, a slightly enhanced Jump action, and the Inner Magic feature. At the start of the day (or as a bonus action a number of times equal to your proficiency bonus), you choose one of three perks.

You might want advantage on Charisma checks and advantage against being Frightened. Or maybe you'd prefer an extra 10ft of speed and swimming that doesn't cost extra movement. Alternatively, you can gain temporary HP equal to your proficiency bonus, as well as advantage on Athletics and Acrobatics checks. These are generalist powers that'd suit pretty much any class, but dexterous smooth talkers like the Rogue and Bard probably benefit best. 

Eladrin

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three ability scores
Best forDruid, Cleric
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes (2018)

The Eladrin 5e are Elves that specifically come from the Feywild, and their appearance and abilities are tied to a particular season. An Eladrin might change seasons over their life or always remain the same.

Like many Elves, Eladrin have advantage on saving throws against the charmed condition. Plus, an Eladrin can teleport 30ft as a bonus action and immediately gain a particular benefit granted by their season. We're particularly keen on Spring, which lets you teleport another creature instead of yourself. Eladrin also have proficiency in Perception, and they can enter a trance instead of sleeping, finishing a long rest in just four hours.

Teleportation is an excellent ability for any character that can't do so already. Since Eladrin also have a natural lean towards Wisdom-based skills, we recommend playing a Druid or Cleric. However, thanks to their custom ability scores, an Eladrin is suitable for any class you like.

Faerie

SizeSmall
Speed30ft (walking and flying)
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three ability scores
Best forRogue, Druid
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022)

Agile, mystical, and tricksy, a Fairy 5e is gifted with spellcasting and enormous wings that let them fly as fast as they can walk. None of their spellcasting options are game-breakers, in our opinion - Druidcraft, Faerie Fire, and Enlarge/Reduce are all a bit situational. But they're a nice bonus for characters that can't otherwise cast them already, even if you can only use them once per long rest.

Fairies make a suitable species for most builds, though their Flight doesn't work with medium or heavy armor, so bear that in mind. We'd recommend one that'll really benefit from flight - like the agile Rogue or a Druid armed with ranged area-of-effect spells.

Firbolg

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three ability scores
Best forRogue
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

The Firbolg 5e is a distant relation of the Giants. They bear some physical resemblance to their ancestors (and they do count as a Large creature when determining how much they can push, drag, lift, or carry), but they have more expertise in magic than brute strength.

They innately know how to Detect Magic 5e and Disguise Self, with fewer restrictions than the average spellcaster. As a bonus action, a Firbolg can also turn invisible until their next turn or attack begins. And their ties to the woods mean they have limited influence over beasts, plants, and other vegetation.

While all this forest flavor may draw you to the Druid or Ranger, we argue that the Rogue is a far better option for Firbolg players. Invisibility, disguises, and advantage on beast-based Charisma checks all play into what a Rogue does best.

Genasi

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three ability scores
Best forCleric, Fighter
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Elemental Evil Player's Companion (2015)

The offspring of genies and mortals, Genasi are elemental beings that manifest the power of planar magic within their blood. Although they closely resemble humans, a Genasi's elemental heritage is clearly visible.

Their gameplay abilities are almost entirely defined by their subraces.

  • Air Genasi can naturally cast the Levitate spell and are resistant to lightning damage;
  • Earth Genasi get a free cast of Pass Without Trace every long rest and can walk across rough terrain for no penalty;
  • Fire Genasi are resistant to fire and know the Produce Flame cantrip from level one;
  • Water Genasi have acid resistance, are amphibious, and can cast the Shape Water cantrip.

Despite these differences, none of the subraces is especially fixed to just one specific class. The Cleric 5e has subclasses that work with the Air Genasi and Fire Genasi, while the Earth Genasi offers minor benefits to martial classes like the Fighter.
