Best forWizard, Artificer
SourcebooksGuildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

Vedalken 5e are partially amphibious creatures who, apart from their blue skin and lack of hair, closely resemble tall humans. Their most powerful ability isn't particularly flavorful, but it has an explosive mechanical effect. Vedalken have advantage on all Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws, meaning they're particularly well-defended against magical effects.

Vedalken can also breathe underwater for up to one hour (once per long rest), but this ability pales in comparison with that first trait. Protection against magic is a buff for pretty much any D&D character, after all.

If you need help narrowing down your choices, look to the Vedalken's proficiencies for suggestions. The species is proficient in an extra tool, plus one skill from this list: Arcana, History, Investigation, Medicine, Performance, and Sleight of Hand. This implies a slight advantage for Intelligence-based casters and skill-focused characters - though a Vedalken Barbarian is still perfectly viable.

Verdan

SizeSmall or medium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 Constitution
Best forSorcerer, Warlock, Bard
SourcebooksAcquisitions Incorporated (2019)

Introduced by Acquisitions Incorporated, the Verdan 5e evolved from goblinoids, though they're often confused for Half-Elves. Whatever their origin, they're best known for their ability to speak telepathically with any creature they can see within 30 feet.

Verdan are also proficient in Persuasion, as well as Wisdom and Charisma saving throws. They're an excellent choice for Charisma casters, though many characters could take advantage of that extra protection against spells.

We'd recommend choosing the Verdan if your preferred class is a bit squishy. Their Black Blood Healing ability allows them to reroll a 1 or 2 on a Hit Dice roll, which will help keep you on your feet between fights.

Warforged

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Constitution, +1 one other score
Best forArtificer, Barbarian, Cleric
SourcebooksEberron: Rising from the Last War (2019)

Members of the Warforged 5e race were once mindless automaton soldiers in the DnD setting of Eberron, but at some point, they gained sentience. Now they're ready to join an adventuring party, armed with their newfound emotions and an artificial body that's ideal for soaking up damage.

Warforged don't need to do pesky mortal things like eat, drink, breathe, or sleep, but they do require rest and healing like any other humanoid. Being made of wood and metal, they're less affected by poisons and they're blessed with a boosted armor class. They can also meld their DnD armor of choice to their body so enemies can't remove it.

To learn more about the Warforged 5e, here's our full guide to the species. 

Yuan-ti

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAny
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

Part human and part snake, the Yuan-ti 5e can often be distinguished by their serpent eyes, noses, or tongues. These snake-like features come with plenty of perks, including Darkvision, resistance to poison damage, and advantage on rolls against the poisoned condition.

Yuan-ti also gain serpentine spellcasting powers, meaning they can cast Poison Spray, Suggestion, and Animal Friendship (though that last one only works on snakes).

Any adventurer can benefit from the Yuan-ti's handy resistances, but these species traits are a little underwhelming, and none lend themselves well to a particular class. If we were going purely on flavor, we'd make a Swarmkeeper Ranger who can summon an army of slithering friends.

Got a D&D character in mind already? Here are the best DnD campaigns and DnD one shots you could play them in. We can also recommend some other tabletop RPGs to try if you want to go beyond D&D.

title: Hobby Build Academy: Tools for Dioramas
content:
Welcome back to Hobby Build Academy! I'm your host, Professor Marcy, joined as always by my helpful assistant Elly! This time, we're taking a look at how to get started with building dioramas; perhaps inspired by our trip to the hobby show last week, we've started looking into the best ways to get started with making displays and dioramas that are great for posing and displaying Gunpla, or other models, in! Some of these certainly overlap with miniature board building and display making, so if you're familiar with that, or actually have never done either, then perhaps some of these tips are going to be very helpful for you in general! There's actually a lot of pretty easy ways to make an effective display and diorama board, and although it may sound like it, you can do it fairly inexpensively in a lot of cases (as long as you realize you may be buying some supplies for the long haul).

This is also about a close as we've come to discussing modeling in the sense of model trains and other scale items, so I will preface this by saying that if you happen to have a hobby store near you that specializes in model trains, you're going to be well served by likely going there first and seeing what's available. A good number of items are pretty widely available just about anywhere, be it hobby stores or even a general department store, and of course, there are plenty of online shops that can help serve your needs. So, we're going to separate this list into different categories to help make things a bit more useful for referencing.

General Supplies

Marcy: So the first category is general supplies. These are things you'll probably be able to source from art and hobby stores, and maybe even other places if you get creative; online resources are also going to do you a lot of good when it comes down to finding some of these items. I also think I'd suggest that you try and think about where you are going to store some of this ahead of time, as some of these items are going to come in bulk or larger sizes that would make it quite a waste to get rid of after just one use!

Elly: I think this list was filled with things you've actually had for quite a while, too, huh?

Marcy: Well, when I was more into building, painting and otherwise working with miniatures, I was very much taken with detailed basing and getting creative. That was really an extension of having done some model kit work when I was younger, and it was actually the part of minis I liked the most.

Marcy: I painted this quite a few years ago, for example.

Elly: When we researched this list, these items were things that I was pretty surprised at the amount of options that are available.

Ground Cover

Don't mix these up with your spices. You do use spices, right?

Marcy: Ground Cover is essentially the material you use to make, well, the ground of whatever display you're working with. As romantic and creative as it seems, you can't really just go grab dirt, rocks, and plants from your yard and use them on permanent displays, at least not without quite a bit of extra work to make them safe. So, Ground Cover products are what you'll want to look for in order to create the illusion of grass, sand, dirt, or similar. Also, it is important to remember scaling and size.

Elly: I think it was kind of interesting to note that Gundam models aren't really as big as they seem, especially when you work with HG kits, but also that to make the scaling match with the in-universe scale, they're also a lot smaller than it might seem. When I was looking into it, it seems that most models are closer to N Scale. So, I think it would look pretty strange to have rocks or plants from your yard that don't match the size of what you're working with; a single blade of glass would look really weird next to a Gunpla!

Marcy: So, this is not meant to be sponsored, but if you are familiar with model trains, you may already know this brand, but Woodland Scenics is probably one of the best overall places to look for Ground Cover. They make quite a lot of types, and they all come in a somewhat iconic shaker bottle that helps you control the flow of your cover (and if you are familiar with kitchen work, they're basically large sized spice canisters).

Elly: Also, Ballast is the term used for rock debris in trains, and they make for great rock accents and for rocky/sandy effects on a display.

Foam Cutter

Not an endorsement, just look for something like this.

Elly: Something we learned looking at displays and dioramas is that you are likely going to work with, or want to consider working with, various types of foam. These are great for making elevation, and can even be used to create a scene of mountains, hills, or the like. Foam cutters come in a lot of different types; you can use a hand saw with some of them, or even a box cutter or hobby knife, but a very easy to use and fairly cheap tool are hot wire cutters. These come in a variety of sizes, brands, and quality, but the basic idea behind them is that a wire apparatus is heated, which then cuts through the foam by melting it.

Marcy: You should do this in a well ventilated place or with a mouth cover, by the way; I've worked with foam cutters in the past for costume work, and melted styrofoam stinks.

Elly: We were able to find a good number of these in few stores, including Amazon, and other hobby stores, so they're not very difficult to find. Also, they seem to run around 15~20 USD, depending on where you look.

Elmer's Glue / School / Project Glue

You know. This stuff.

Elly: Whatever you want to call it, the basic, white glue that you used as a kid is going to be a lot of use to you in making a display board. Aside from helping you affix things like your ground cover, foliage, or other items, you can actually do some pretty cool things with glue if you apply it, let it dry, and create textures with it that you can then paint over. You'll want to work with the basic stuff here, since you aren't working with the models themselves; essentially you're not looking for plastic cement or super-glue for the model, so you don't have to get too over the top with what you're using.

Specialized Supplies

Marcy: for these items, I would consider these things you'd likely find at a hobby store primarily, and may even have to consider looking for them on specialized retailers that have a focus on modeling. Woodland Scenics is getting another shout-out here, but you don't have to rely only on them; just that they are one of the more well known and available brands that make it fairly easy to get most of what you need in one place.

Foam

Elly: Specifically, we're talking about the type of foam you'll want to get for hobby work, which is going to depend on the type, size, and scale of the display you're using. In most cases, you aren't going to be working with average pieces of styrofoam like you might find in an electronics package, although if you wanted to get real creative and have some lying around, you can certainly experiment with it using the foam cutter!

Marcy: A lot of hobby foam is a bit smoother than commercial styrofoam, which helps give it a much better overall outer appearance, but there's some things you can do to get around that or get more creative with it, which we'll touch on. But, yes, finding foam in hobby stores will be where you might want to look. There are a lot of shapes and varieties, and you may even want to consider looking into the foam used for various art supplies or products, even the type used for flower arrangement.

Plaster Cloth / Plaster of Paris

Marcy: So here, you've got a few options; you can make your own, if you're familiar with and comfortable with working with the material, such as Plaster of Paris, but you can also buy premade Plaster Cloths that can be laid onto foam or other surfaces that help eliminate the 'foam' look, as well as protect the foam itself. Most model train layouts have plaster of some form over the foam, which can then be painted, textured, and otherwise decorated to help make it look more realistic and create the illusion of whatever biome you've opted to decorate.

Elly: Plaster of Paris is pretty inexpensive compared to the plaster cloth items, but the trade-off is that you are likely going to buy a lot of Plaster of Paris that you'll need to properly store once you're done with using it; when I was looking, I think the most available sizes I could go pick up at hardware stores were either 4lb bags or 25lbs, both of which are a lot more than I would probably need!

Cork

How to spackle over cork layers

Elly: Now, cork isn't really that hard to obtain, but it does have a bit of difficulty curve when you're using it for things that aren't just a plain, flat surface.

Marcy: Yes, while many Warhammer players are probably familiar with cork boards for the flat surface of a display board, working with cork beyond that can present some interesting textures and options, but also a lot of frustration. First of all, you generally only get cork in either wine corks or the style used for coasters or boards, which are all pretty thin. That said, you can do some fun things with cork if you cut and apply it, creating things like rough edges or small elevations that will have jagged textures (or, if you plaster or even just glue over it with ground cover, can just help break up flat terrain).

Acrylics for Texturing

Marcy: perhaps something slightly familiar to people who have made playing boards and larger scale items for gaming that have a water feature, but there are numerous acrylic materials you can use to help create things like the illusion of water. Although there are some far more intricate things that can be done with pouring various materials, many of these texture acrylics are made to be applied to the surface of something and then help give the illusion of water, waves, mud, or similar. As mentioned before, this isn't sponsored, but I don't think I've ever used anything other than Vallejo textures and Woodland Scenic textures in my life, and would probably suggest starting with those. They work great, they're easy to find, and generally they're fairly inexpensive.

Pre-Made Options

Marcy: So, you always have one other option: you can actually get a lot of pre-made items if you work within N-Scale, at least for most HG and MG gunpla. This means that if you don't really want to do the DIY aspects, but do want to make a cool looking display in a bookshelf or detolf, you can always look to buy N-Scale items like terrain, foliage, buildings, rocks, and all sorts of things. You can always consider things like aquarium decorations too for rocks, but just beware that some of those look very fake and plastic-y in order to be safe for use in aquariums and terrariums.

Wrap-Up

Hopefully, you've found some fun ideas here if you want to make something a bit more dynamic and fun to display your models in. Whether that is for a model show, or just your own edification, hopefully these items are good places for you to start and consider; in general, I think we'd say that the overall tip we'd want to give is that these items are not that hard to obtain or work with, and of the things listed here, plaster of paris is maybe the messiest, but still very simple!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: The best MTG Commanders October 2026
content:
The Commander is the legendary creature that leads your other 99 cards into battle in games of EDH: they dictate the colors you can include in your deck, and shape your overall strategy. If you're shopping for new options, our tried-and-tested guide to the best MTG commanders recommends plenty that reliably secure wins and are extremely fun to play.

Wizards of the Coast introduces more legendary creatures with each year of new MTG sets, but this guide will help you keep up with the latest releases and meta shifts. If you want to get really competitive, you'll be better served by our dedicated cEDH tier list. Or, if you're just starting out with this format, we'd recommend starting out with MTG commander precon decks instead.

Latest MTG commanders news in October

The list below covers the best MTG commanders that have already been released. However, spoiler season shows us spicy new options long before they go to print. If you want the most up-to-date MTG commander announcements, here's a brief summary of October's biggest news.

The big announcements have all been Marvel-flavored. Four Darkhold Destiny commander decks have been confirmed for next year's Universes Beyond set. Among those spoilers, we're most intrigued by Gargantos, the Endbringer, who can get suitably massive depsite its 0/0 statline.

After Darkhold, we know that all future releases will come with four commander decks. That's a huge amount of choice in 2027!

Top commanders MTG:

  • Atraxa, Praetors' Voice
  • Edgar Markov
  • Vivi Ornitier
  • Teval, the Balanced Scale
  • Baylen, the Haymaker
  • The Necrobloom
  • Kenrith, The Returned King
  • Muldrotha, The Gravetide
  • Tymna The Weaver
  • The Gitrog Monster
  • Isshin, Two Heavens As One
  • Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow
  • Sauron, The Dark Lord
  • The Ur Dragon
  • Kaalia Of The Vast
  • Lathril, Blade Of The Elves
  • Pantlaza, Sun Favored
  • Shroofus Sproutshire
  • Atraxa, Grand Unifier

Atraxa, Praetors' Voice

While not quite the dominant force she was in 2016, Atraxa, Praetors' Voice still makes for a top commander. Her proliferate ability opens up all kinds of avenues and has only gotten more flexible as Wizards experiments with new types of counters like shield and stun.

Atraxa is a really great commander to experiment with because her ability and color identity mean you can explore about six different themes. You could make a pretty standard +1/+1 counter deck, or go the opposite route with -1/-1 counters. You could be really unpleasant and run with poison counters, or create a superfriends deck full of planeswalkers.Whatever route you go, you're probably going to want more effects that proliferate, so cards like Ezuri, Stalker of Spheres and Tekuthal, Inquiry Dominus are a perfect fit. They also often lend themselves to a Phyrexian theme!

Game Changers for Atraxa, Praetor's Voice

  • Fierce Guardianship
  • Force of Will

Edgar Markov

The Commander 2017 set was all about tribal decks, each focused on a single creature type: cats, wizards, dragons, and vampires. Edgar Markov led the cats - no, sorry, the vampires deck - and quickly rose to the status of top commander. While the card got horribly pricey as a result, a reprint in Innistrad Remastered has made him a little less silly to buy.

With the ability to create a swarm of little nippers, then pump them up each time he attacks, Edgar naturally works best in a horde-style deck that can swiftly overwhelm opponents. Mardu colors give you access to all the top removal cards, and best of all, Edgar's eminence ability makes him useful from the command zone, where he can churn out mini-mes in safety.

You then need stuff to do with all your vampire tokens, like buffing them up or sacrificing them for card draw with Skullclamp and draining your opponent with Blood Artist.

Game Changers for Edgar Markov

  • Braids, Cabal Minion

Vivi Ornitier

MTG's Final Fantasy set was stuffed with legendary creatures, but Vivi Ornitier is the real standout for Commander players. He grows more powerful every time you cast a non-creature spell, and that power in turn fuels an incredibly versatile mana-making ability.

Vivi can be hard to keep in play due to his notoriety (he did terrible things in Standard) but on the bright side, his mana cost is so low that it shouldn't be too hard to bring him back. Keep him on the board long enough, and Vivi becomes a powerful attacker in his own right, but his real value lies in the win conditions you can create with the killer combination of free mana and pinging. A Curiosity-type card also makes this guy a card draw machine.

With Vivi, your game plan might be a spellslinger or storm build - setting up until the perfect turn allows you to combo off. Alternatively, you could go all in on pingers, and aim to whittle your opponents down with a million tiny cuts.

Game Changers for Vivi

  • Cyclonic Rift
  • Mystical Tutor
  • Rhystic Study

Teval, the Balanced Scale

Teval, the Balanced Scale offers fantastic value, especially for a precon commander. This spicy spirit dragon has seen its popularity soar since Tarkir: Dragonstorm, and no wonder. It's a consistent source of land and tokens whose self-mill strategies synergize with a variety of decks.

Obviously, a straightforward graveyard deck is the first place to go. You want cards entering and leaving your graveyard as often as possible to trigger Teval's ability. After that though, you could consider a lands-matter sub-theme, playing multiple lands a turn to stack up the triggers. You could look to get the most from your tokens with zombie tribal cards too.

Your biggest problem will be defending Teval, who has no protection against removal, will suffer when cards are exiled, and who must constantly jump into the fray of battle.

Gamechangers for Teval

  • Force of Will
  • Fierce Guardianship
  • Gifts Ungiven

Baylen, the Haymaker

If you love using tokens, Baylen, the Haymaker might just be the best commander in all of Magic: The Gathering history, but he has surprising depth - this isn't just your typical go-wide tokens leader.

You wouldn't necessarily know that from the first step of your gameplan though: you begin by amassing a token army. They don't all have to be creatures, you can use treasure or food as well. But after this step is where the rabbit is flexible.

If you want to win with commander damage, you can tap your tokens to buff Baylen up with counters and swing for lethal. He turns four tokens into three +1/+1 counters, so even without built-in protection, this is very doable.

Alternatively, you can use your tokens for mana and card draw. That lets you dig through your deck and cast other key pieces that will help you convert tokens into victory.

I'll lastly add that there are few better commanders to pick for an Hare Apparent deck, if you just want to overwhelm your foes with a lupine legion.

Gamechangers for Baylen

  • Smothering Tithe
  • Biorhythm
  • Aura Shards

The Necrobloom

The Necrobloom is easy for opponents to underestimate. On its early turns, it doesn't seem to achieve much - play a land, fetch a land, create a puny plant token. However, if left undisturbed for long enough, it's landfall antics will start to cause serious problems.

As soon as seven types of land are under your control, you can start building a zombie army, all while blocking with your chunky commander their numerous plant buddies. Dredge is on hand to bring back any crucial lands, and it opens up plenty of interactions that keep The Necrobloom's tokens-and-landfall schtick feeling interesting.

Mass land-reanimation is particularly deadly in this deck, creating a huge horde that has to be dealt with in one turn cycle, else it's game over.

Gamechangers for the Necrobloom

  • Field of the Dead
  • Crop Rotation

Kenrith, The Returned King

Five-color commanders are some of the strongest because they allow you to use any card in the game. That means ultimate flexibility. As a result, they're a little controversial, since many lend themselves to less focused strategies and decks, where you just want to cram in all the best cards in your collection.

But we think that's as valid a playstyle as any - and it's hard to pass up jack-of-all-trades commanders when they're as good as Kenrith, the Returned King. Kenrith shines because all of his abilities are useful, and some are invaluable. You only need white mana to cast him, so you can have him out on the field and gradually unlock new abilities as you play new lands.

He's a top commander for those still learning how to play Magic The Gathering's most popular format, since you can experiment to your heart's content, and it's hard to go too wrong. Synergy is not required - just brute strength!

Gamechangers for Kenrith

  • Coalition Victory
  • Gifts Ungiven
  • Fierce Guardianship

Muldrotha, The Gravetide

Do you hate it when your opponents blow up your stuff? Then Muldrotha, the Gravetide is the top commander for you. Allowing you to play one card of each permanent type from your graveyard each and every turn, this noxious elemental turns your graveyard into an extension of your hand.

Unfortunately, with a high cost and incredible ability, Muldrotha is one of those commanders that attracts removal like a magnet. On the bright side, her Sultai colors (black, green and blue) give you access to a ton of power outside of her own impressive strength, including excellent creatures, removal, and card draw.

And when you do manage to protect her for long enough to make good use of her resurrection powers, your opponents are going to have a bad time.

Gamechangers for Muldrotha

  • Gifts Ungiven
  • Intuition
  • Fierce Guardianship

Tymna The Weaver

Tymna the Weaver may not look like much from the outset - sure, she draws cards when you hit people, whatever. But never underestimate the power of friendship. Tymna is a top commander choice because she has the Partner ability, which - like Tymna herself - was introduced in the Commander 2016 set. That means you can pair her up with any legendary creature that also has 'Partner' to give them joint leadership of your commander deck.

Two commanders are better than one, since they unlock new card options and new synergies, as well as ensuring you always have a creature to play out. Tymna makes this list simply because she's one of the most versatile creatures with the Partner ability. The card draw she provides will be valuable, whatever strategy you're going for.

Tymna the Weave is most often paired up with the merfolk card Thrasios, Triton Hero. That's because this combination gives you access to four colors and two commanders with generically powerful abilities. They don't make Partners like this anymore, and for good reason.

Gamechangers for Tymna

  • Thassa's Oracle
  • Orcish Bowmasters

The Gitrog Monster

A froggy chap with a winning smile, The Gitrog Monster has a series of unique, versatile abilities that make for a powerful MTG commander. It lets you play more lands, allowing for copious ramping, and you get to draw cards each time you put lands in the graveyard.

Cards like Crucible of Worlds will help you bring valuable lands back to the battlefield so you can sacrifice them again and again for endless utility. Even a simple Evolving Wilds can be extremely useful for Gitrog.

Whether you're using discard outlets or sacrificing lands, there's plenty of ways to generate absurd value with this top commander. You can also abuse infinite combos, which makes The Gitrog Monster a viable combo deck in cEDH.

Gamechangers for the Gitrog Monster

  • Crop Rotation
  • Field of the Dead
  • Glacial Chasm

Isshin, Two Heavens As One

Isshin, Two Heavens as One has just one simple ability, but its elegance and simplicity belies its power. This high tech samurai doubles up all your attack triggers, letting you generate absurd value whenever you swing at your opponents.

Not the best commander for anyone who likes playing a slower, defensive game, Isshin wants you to strike hard and strike fast. While all Isshin decks want to attack, this is another commander that you can build in a few ways, as there are loads of strong creature cards to choose from, and plenty of room for building up subthemes.

Even better, his very affordable mana cost means you don't have to worry too much about removal spells, as you can play Isshin, Two Heavens as One several times without it becoming too taxing.

Gamechangers for Isshin

  • The One Ring
  • Jeska's Will
  • Teferi's Protection

Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow

If you like ninjas, then Magic: The Gathering has a brilliant commander option. With Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow, your whole deal is striking with low-cost, evasive creatures, then launching your commander into play with ninjitsu, and reaping the rewards: plenty of card draw, and plenty of pain.

The best thing about Yuriko is, as long as you have an unblocked creature, you can always get her into play for two mana. This is huge. It means no matter how many times your opponents deal with your commander, it's always a threat.

The rest of your deck is not so resilient to a board wipe - and a board wipe can seriously set you back, though you can usually hold up a counterspell or two to protect your ninja army. Yuriko makes for a top budget commander deck too - little unblockable guys don't tend to cost too much.

Gamechangers for a Yuriko deck

  • Force of Will
  • Consecrated Sphinx
  • Cyclonic Rift

Sauron, The Dark Lord

A six-cost commander in Grixis, a color combo not exactly known for ramp, is a tough sell. However, if you can hang on and play Sauron, the Dark Lord, you're all set to have a great time. He's a self-fueling engine.

Once Sauron comes down, he starts to roll an unstoppable boulder at your opponent. No one wants to pay the ward cost to get rid of him, and every time anyone casts a spell, you get another Amass trigger.

Soon, your Orcs will be enormous, something on your board will be very hard to block, and you'll be drawing several cards a turn. Sauron works great with several cards from the Lord of the Rings set, which have a very high power level. And you can bring in all the old Amass cards from War of the Spark, too.

He can also reliably pitch your hand into your graveyard, which can make a good setup for graveyard strategies - whether you're trying to get an Underworld Breach / Lion's Eye Diamond loop going for a combo, or just want to reanimate something huge.

Gamechangers for a Sauron deck

  • Demonic Tutor
  • Lion's Eye Diamond
  • Underworld Breach

The Ur Dragon

The Ur Dragon offers a simple strategy, but it's still powerful enough to stampede casual commander tables (and steal a few more competitive wins, too). Its Eminence keyword means that, whether this card is on the battlefield or not, all your MTG dragons are one mana cheaper. The plan should be clear from here - fill your deck with huge, hard-hitting fliers and let rip.

The Ur Dragon is very expensive to get on the battlefield. However, it's a 10/10 flyer that allows you to draw cards equal to the number of your attacking dragons. Even better, you can then place a permanent from your hand onto the battlefield for free.

There are plenty of cards that synergize with The Ur Dragon's matter-of-fact battle plan. Prioritize those that give you extra benefits for playing dragons onto the battlefield or that can make these mana-hungry creatures even cheaper. You'll also need a solid ramp plan if you want your enormous dragons to get off the ground.

Gamechangers for The Ur Dragon

  • Mana Vault
  • Ancient Tomb
  • Chrome Mox

Kaalia Of The Vast

Kaalia of the Vast has been considered a top commander almost since the format's inception. Even today, this card's powers are impressive. Kaalia is a four-cost Mardu commander with flying and the ability to add a card from your hand to the battlefield whenever she attacks. That card must be an Angel, Demon, or Dragon creature, and it's automatically tapped and attacking along with Kaalia.

This is a ferociously fast way to cheat flying threats onto the field. If you can give Kaalia haste, your chosen commander can start handing out freebies as early as turn four. Lightning Greaves, Swiftwood Boots, and Dragon Tempest are your friend here.

Naturally, you'll want a deck full of angels, demons, and dragons to back Kaalia up. You should also leave space for problem-solving cards. Kaalia is a veteran of the competitive commander scene, so you can expect many players to have a game plan when she shows up - removal, removal, and removal.

Gamechangers for a Kaalia of the Vast deck

  • Teferi's Protection
  • Demonic Tutor
  • Imperial Seal


Lathril, Blade Of The Elves

As one of the oldest and best-established creature types in all of Magic: The Gathering, elves have long been a super powerful tribe. There's just been so much time for Wizards to print good elves, and there are now so many of them standing around pouting and hugging trees that it's almost too easy to make a strong elves deck. Just find the cards with the pointy ears and chuck a bunch in.

Lathril, Blade of the Elves is a Kaldheim commander who provides a nice bit of edge for elves decks by adding black to their color identity. This top commander also gives you a powerful new win condition, letting you use your elvish army to drain your opponents for huge chunks of life.

Lathril gives you plenty of options. You can build her to be a classic green elves deck, which ramps up quickly to a critical mass of creatures and then pulls out one of umpteen win conditions. But you can also create a combo style deck that relies on untappers to build up infinite mana, or uses them with Lathril herself to close out the game.

Gamechangers for Lathril

  • Natural Order
  • Survival of the Fittest
  • Gaea's Cradle

Pantlaza, Sun-Favored

Open the door, get on the floor, and prepare to walk the dinosaur, with one of the most popular MTG commanders of recent years. There's a good reason Pantlaza Sun-Favored sees so much play. Coming out of one of the best precon decks ever released, this raptor is a top commander choice if you just want to throw around some big stompy dinosaurs.

Pantlaza's Discover ability means that each dinosaur you cast has the potential to trigger a cascade, letting you fetch up one or potentially more other random dinosaurs from your deck (worst case scenario you hit a mana rock or something). It feels great to start a turn with just your commander on board, and end it with a herd of colossal reptiles whose approaching roars tell your opponents that you are very much the threat. Just make sure you pack enough ramp!

The randomness of this ability might be frustrating to some, but for others it'll ensure their deck always feels fresh.

Gamechangers for Pantlaza

  • Teferi's Protection
  • Farewell
  • Gaea's Cradle

Shroofus Sproutsire

We're not sure if Shroofus Sproutsire truly deserves to be on a list of all-time top commanders, but we've included him as an added extra because we couldn't bear to upset the lil' guy. He's certainly one of the best Jumpstart 2025 Commanders at any rate.

You're always going to have to put a bit of work in to land a hit with this commander, but once you get the ball rolling it's going to move very very fast. While he'd probably work better as Slimefoot's right hand man, this creature will feel like having Scute Swarm in your command zone.

Gamechangers for Shroofus Sproutshire

  • Gaea's Cradle
  • Natural Order
  • Seedborn Muse

Atraxa, Grand Unifier

Alright, Atraxa, Grand Unifier comes with an eye-watering mana cost, and it doesn't have the explosive proliferate powers of our other favored Atraxa commander. However, Grand Unifier offers heaps of power and versatility.

This is a mighty 7/7 commander with flying, vigilance, deathtouch, and lifelink. If you can keep Atraxa in play, it'll obliterate opposing forces, dole out enormous chunks of commander damage, and keep you well-defended in the meantime.

Perhaps more important is Atraxa's enters-the-battlefield ability. This allows you to reveal ten cards from the top of your library. For each card type among those, you can put one card of each revealed type into your hand. The rest go on the bottom of your library in a random order.

This is a commander with fairly generic powers that can feel a bit 'jack of all trades, master of none'. However, this also makes Atraxa suitable for a variety of deck types, from Blink to Phyrexian Typal.

Gamechangers for Atraxa, Grand Unifier

  • Thassa's Oracle
  • Grand Arbiter Augustin IV
  • Force of Will

Thorin, King of Durin's Folk

One of our recent favorites, Thorin, King of Durin's Folk is the new hot dwarf on the block. Lovers of typal decks, stuffed to the brim with Treasure and Equipment, are in for a treat. Thorin creates a Treasure token whenever he or another Dwarf enters, and he gives other Dwarves +1/+1 for each artifact token you control.

It's a simple formula: spam tokens, buff Dwarves, profit. Despite its simplicity, it's tremendous fun to build and play. There are plenty of Dwarves who can be their own source of artifact tokens, including obvious champion Magda.

Gamechangers for Thorin, King of Durin's Folk

  • Magda, Brazen Outlaw
  • Gloin, Dwarf Emissary
  • Smaug the Magnificent

title: Ancient MTG card sees 220% price spike thanks to powerful life gain synergies
content:
The Magic: The Gathering card Lifegift has not so much jumped up in price as sauntered vaguely upwards. This card was worth about $7.30 at the beginning of the year, but rose to $10 gradually over the past nine months. Then, through September and October, it climbed all the way to $23.45.

A rather old card from the 2004 MTG set Champions of Kamigawa, Lifegift has a very straightforward effect. It's a three mana enchantment which states that whenever a land comes into play (under anyone's control) you gain a single point of life.

Obviously, in two-player Constructed formats that would be incredibly anemic, but in Commander it's a lot better - especially if anyone is ramping, popping down multiple lands a turn. It's especially great for decks that want a lot of separate instances of lifegain, to trigger effects, but don't actually care how much life is being gained.

Since this card has never seen a reprint and hails from the early 2000s, we can assume there aren't loads of copies in circulation, which oftentimes means a card is ripe to blow up when just the right synergy comes along.

It seems like Kwia Vigorbloom is the key commander driving this spike. Kwia has an absurd mana ramping power that effectively makes Black Lotus tokens when you gain life, but thankfully it only activates once per turn.

That means gaining life on your opponents' turns is absolutely essential. The soul sisters (Soul Warden, Soul's Attendant and their ilk) are must-haves, but if you wanted a harder-to-remove version, you could do worse than Lifegift.

It's especially great because the enchantment's lifegain is tied to something unusual. Say you have Soul Warden and Essence Warden in play, you'll still only get one Kwia trigger if your opponent plays a creature. But if they don't commit a body to the board, you're losing out on a Black Lotus. Disaster! Far better to diversify your triggers: run Lifegift instead, and increase your chances of grabbing 12 extra mana per turn cycle.

Lifegift is only included in 20% of Kwia decks logged on EDHREC, and I'm surprised that's been enough to trigger the spike. But perhaps other lifegain commanders have run the reserves dry (topical) over the years, as this card also saw lots of play with Bilbo in the original LOTR set, and this year it was played in Blech decks.

Once upon a time, Lifegift would have sold for far less - for a long while this was a bargain bulk rare, priced at less than a dollar. That all changed though in 2021, with Strixhaven School of Mages.

Dina, which uses lifegain to whittle your opponents' health away, was a very popular commander in this set. And since her Golgari lifegain makes all the white lifegain cards unavailable, Lifegift was a life-gaining gift that Dina players couldn't overlook.

title: Eldfall Chronicles is a tense skirmish wargame that feels like a duel between D&D parties
content:
Wargamers in America might suddenly have noticed Eldfall Chronicles appearing on store shelves, a fantasy skirmish wargame with a broad range of arresting miniatures that promises both PVP and PvE combat. Having built up steam in continental Europe over the last three years, it's finally available via US retail chains - I've been testing it to see what it has to offer.

I've read Eldfall Chronicle's rules, messed around with the army-building app, built and painted minis, and tried a couple of test games. Take these as first impressions - I'm not yet confident whether or not it deserves a place on our guide to the best miniature wargames when that finally gets its overdue overhaul. But I am itching to find more time to test the game.

The product

There are a couple of two player starter sets available, each of which come with rules, two faction starter sets of four models each, an NPC water elemental, cards, and tokens. Just about any pack you buy with three or more models in it constitutes a playable party, and the rules and unit cards are all available to download for free online. There's also a good quality army building app.

As well as the skirmish wargame, there's also an Eldfall Chronicles dungeon crawler system called Northern Winds. The miniatures are fully compatible with the skirmish game, and there's even a card pack to bring the models from the first wave of Eldfall releases into the dungeon crawler. I haven't looked at the dungeon crawler at all, but it's an interesting alternative entry point to the skirmish game.

Eldfall Chronicles' miniatures are fantastic. The aesthetic is clean high fantasy, with a bit of Wuxia and anime influence in the mix. The entire range is cast in Unicool, a resin that holds incredible detail without being too brittle. Construction was easy and didn't require any knife work beyond cleaning up flash. The level of detail on the infantry figures is so fine it's somewhat beyond my ability to paint, but the monster miniatures hit a sweet spot where they're genuinely relaxing to work on.

Now, the minis aren't flawless. There's some resin droop on spears and sword blades, which I've been able to fix by placing the bent bit into boiling water, reshaping it, and then cooling it off. A particularly spindly mage's bident snapped during some rough handling. It was a clean break that I could fix, and I attribute it to the model's design rather than the material - I'd expect a HIPs piece that was just as thin to be just as breakable. I get the sense the designers were pushing the detail of what the molds could produce, but have since become a bit more cautious about what will survive on the tabletop, because the newer models are more robust.

The rules writing is fairly clear, and sufficiently well translated into English. There are some naming oddities that I assume come either from the language barrier or an attempt not to directly copy another game - for instance there's a 'crouched' state in which a model can't engage enemies, is easier to hit in melee, and harder to hit at range, and that feels more like being 'prone' to me. The rules err on the side of brevity rather than clarity, which makes reading them pretty easy, but I expect that - unless the competitive meta takes off - players from different states will develop slightly different readings of them.

The gameplay

Eldfall Chronicles is a very low model-count skirmish game - it's likely that each player will field a party of just four figures. The rules are deep enough that you will still have plenty of decisions to make each turn, and with so few models, every one is critical. It feels like each player is commanding a D&D party of heroes with distinct yet complimentary roles.

There is definitely some D&D in Eldfall's DNA, because the rules are extremely similar to the sci-fi skirmish game Infinity, which evolved out of a heavily modded sci-fi D&D campaign. There are impactful differences between the two games, but existing Infinity players will be able to hop in Eldfall without any trouble.

Like Infinity, the game uses a variant I-Go-U-Go system in which one player takes an active turn with their whole party, while their opponent has a slightly more limited reactive turn to respond to their actions. If you advance and shoot at an enemy you may find them shooting back; try to disengage from combat and they may attack you on the way out; sneaking around behind a character restricts their reactions; and so on.

But a critical difference from Infinity is the way that models activate. In Infinity your 'Order Pool' can be spent to activate just about any model you like as many times as you can afford, allowing powerful attackers to 'go Rambo' or specialists to repeatedly attempt to complete a mission objective. Eldfall Chronicles is a lot more traditional. Each turn, whether you're the active or reactive player, you'll assign a number of activation tokens to each model in your party equal to its Stamina stat - usually that's two tokens.

Each token lets an active model make one activation, consisting of a move and an action like an attack or a spell or a single special move like running, climbing, or jumping; for a reactive model the token gets you one reaction, like a counterattack or dodge.

When you're the active player, even your most powerful heroes can only reliably activate twice. When you're the reactive player, your reactions are a finite resource, and a critical component in your defense against enemy attacks. I felt this most acutely once models were engaged in melee, simply unable to raise their shield or swing their sword because they were out of tokens.

Similar to Infinity, to succeed in an action you need to roll one or more D20s and score equal to or under the relevant stat. When two models lock blades in melee, or one tries to dodge away from the other's hurled spear, both players roll dice, with higher successes cancelling out lower ones.

Every model has a lot of stats, keywords, and unique abilities. While the kits come with printed cards, the web-based party building app feels essential, thanks to the hyperlinked explanations of all those rules. Given you're only managing four models at a time, I found it to be pretty manageable, but there will definitely be an onboarding hurdle as you attempt to learn everyone's capabilities. The payoff is that models feel extremely distinctive and tailored around their role.

I got a feeling for how rich this could make the game early in my first test session, when my Onatoishi - a beast of a samurai - ended up stuck in combat with my opponent's Citadel Guard. The Onatoishi was an unstoppable force, with a massive Offensive melee stat of 16, a powerful greatsword, and thanks to the Armsmaster class and the level three Fencing combat art, the opportunity to roll three dice to strike when attacking. The Citadel Guard was an immovable object, with a Defensive melee stat of 16, the Sentinel class granting it +1 dice with its armor-piercing mace when defending, plus a shield and the level one Fencing combat art which together penalized my Onatoishi's attack rolls by -6.

Did that sound like a lot of keywords and abilities? It is, and I've only mentioned the ones that were relevant to this combat - both models had more abilities besides. But with just four models per side this cognitive load is manageable. While it took a lot of referencing for this initial playthrough, the result felt dramatic - my Onatoishi's onslaught of blows brought to a standstill by the supreme calm of the Citadel Guard.

What's particularly compelling, in terms of list-building, is that models can all receive at least one upgrade. If there were more models in your list it would be obvious that you just make your best fighter a better fighter, your best archer a better archer. With only four models there's a real case to be made that you might be better of upgrading your weaker models or at least diversifying the domains your elites can compete in.

NPC monsters show up in certain scenarios as complicating factors or mission objectives to be killed, and are controlled using AI behaviour cards for both an active and a reactive turn - I've given this a basic test. A battle against a pair of Earth Elementals proved very interesting, since their stats were nothing like regular heroes, with Agility so bad they could never dodge or even perceive enemies not directly in front of them, but Armor that only the strongest weapons could pierce, an lethal attacks. Maneuvering around them to attack them from their blind spot was essential to avoid suffering casualties during my own turn.

Holistically, the Eldfall Chronicles range feels like an effort to make really cool fantasy miniatures and then provide as many ways to play with them as possible. I'm only surprised that there isn't also a TTRPG. If you like the aesthetic, the models are gorgeous - just as well given the price - and my first impressions of the gameplay are very positive.

I received samples of the Empire of Soga vs Helion League starter set, Imperial Banner and Queen's Blade reinforcement packs, and the Earthen Creatures expansion pack, to test. I've built everything, painted some of it, and played with some of that. I'll share some pictures in the Wargamer Discord community when I'm actually satisfied with what I've done!

title: Both cozy and cunning, this new Splendor-like board game is deviously fun
content:
Our Verdict

Yotei achieves a splendid amount with so few mechanics. A few decks of cards, some standees, and a pile of potato tokens are all it takes to craft a cunning game of bluffing, resource management, bidding, and betrayal. Combine that with a cosy, clever theme, and you've got a winning formula. It's not the most replayable gameplay loop, but when games last an hour or less, it never outstays its welcome.

Pros
  • Simple, elegant rules
  • Enthralling mix of mechanics
  • Excellent theme
Cons
  • Limited replayability
  • Some vague rules

I was surprised to learn that Yotei is a debut board game. Huy Pham's first-ever design is so polished, it feels like the work of a veteran. It achieves so much with so little. This is a fantastic mix of bluffing, take-that, resource management, and bidding - all achieved with just a handful of colorful cards and tokens.

'Charming' is a word I use far too often in board game reviews, but it's necessary here. Firstly, because Yotei charms the socks off you from the get-go. It's a cute, compact game about building lovely towns at the foot of Japan's Mt. Yotei. By drafting cards and farming potatoes, you choose which aspects of local culture and natural beauty will pull in the most awe-inspired tourists.

The art is twee, the vibes are cozy, and there's an abundance of nature in the theme. Boom. Charming game.

But also, Charm is the literal currency that wins the game. You and up to three others are competing to earn the most Charm points - little love hearts printed on various cards. Generally, the more valuable a card, the more likely it is to net you Charm.

Let me explain what I mean by 'value'. There are four types of cards in Yotei, and the first three are split into tiers. Tier one represents undeveloped lands and their natural elements. These might offer Charm and additional rewards, but typically, they're the basic building blocks you need to acquire cards from higher tiers. There are three elements a card can offer (mountain, farmland, or forest).

Tier two cards are small developments that offer a low number of Charm points. If you've collected the right mix of elements from land cards, you can create Tourism Developments, Local Produces, or Forest Bounties. These in turn are required to craft specific tier three cards.

These are the fanciest, most expensive developments: Ski Resorts, intriguing Food Culture, and lavish Wilderness. Here's where the big Charm points are on offer. You can only ever acquire two of these cards, though - once someone gets a second tier three card, the game ends, and the person with the most Charm wins.

How do we go about nabbing these cards, then? Each round is split into a Placement Phase and a Harvest Phase. During Placement, you'll take turns placing an adorable standee on the card you intend to grab.

You can place your standee on any face-up card, but you can also turn that card face-down and then claim it. This will give you different rewards at harvest - a basic Forest element for tier-one cards, two potatoes at tier two, or a single popularity point at tier three. Alternatively, you can place your standee on top of the draw deck itself, taking that card, face-down, during Harvest.

As I mentioned, some cards have conditions you must meet to take the card, but you don't have to worry about meeting these until Harvest. However, if a card has a Potato cost, you must place the required number of tokens immediately.

Potatoes may be a humble vegetable, but they're crucial in Yotei. When you're not spending them on placement requirements, you'll use them on bidding cards. Non-bidding cards are automatically claimed by the first player to place a standee, but bidding cards must be won at auction. When you place a standee on a bidding card, you also place a box with a mystery number of potatoes inside. Place the most potatoes, and you win the card during Harvest.

Harvest begins when everyone has placed their three (or, in four-player games, two) standees. The first player resolves all their placements before passing to the next person. If you meet the requirements of a card (and possibly win its bid), you place it in front of your personal privacy screen - it's now yours! So are any rewards in the top-right corner. That's usually Charm points, but it might also be a Mystery card.

Here comes our fourth and final card type. Mystery cards are a random deck of bonuses that you keep hidden and can play at any time. You can cash them in for potatoes, or you can use their special ability. Some give you extra popularity if you still hold them at the end of the game (you've got a max of three at any time). Others let you place two standees at once, shuffle an entire row of cards, freeze cards out of a round, or steal potatoes.

That's Yotei in a nutshell. This small handful of rules creates a delicate dance of bidding, bluffing, management, and take-that. What makes it so compelling is that there is always an interesting decision to make. Even if none of the cards available suit you, you can sabotage a rival by taking the flipside of something you know they covet. Everyone's tiered cards are public knowledge, so you can easily strike them where it hurts.

Even when you don't feel like being dastardly, you've a lot of choices to make about your own town-building. Do you race to claim a tier three card early, knowing you still need to grab a land card to meet its requirements? It's more efficient than building your reserves over several turns, but a canny opponent could block you by claiming the exact card you need. Any player who doesn't meet the requirements of a claimed card returns empty-handed during Harvest.

Additionally, is it better to bid or claim outright on your early turns? Only one person can claim a non-bidding cards, but those bidding boxes are finite, and you might miss out on an essential card unless you hurry.

During all this analysis, you can't forget about potatoes, either. They put a ceiling on your bidding power, and they might slow your progress completely if you can't pay a card's entry requirements. Collecting potatoes is slow, and often inefficient, but it's necessary to stop and refuel now and then.

Here is where I think Yotei's theme really shines. There's a tension between the game's natural elements and its urban development that's captured by a need for both efficient and inefficient turns.

Charming visitors to your village requires fancy ski resorts and festivals, but sometimes, you need to pause and wander the forest, or farm potatoes. The nature of the competition before us has capitalist undertones, but no one can live a truly optimized life, working at full capacity at all times. Yotei tells us that rest is an essential part of growth.

That wholesome message doesn't detract from Yotei's delightful backstabbing, though. This is still a ruthless game of economy. Risk might push you ahead, but it leaves you vulnerable to betrayal, and that can bring your carefully-planned turns crashing down around you. Some might find the high chance of failure frustrating, but it's important to go with the flow. Yotei's board state changes constantly, and there's almost always a chance to recover if you keep a cool head.

Yotei's gameplay loop isn't varied enough to justify back-to-back games, but it makes a fantastic warm-up for any board game night. It has both beauty and bite.

title: Contemptor Kevin's Combat Patrol Issue 70 Review
content:
Issue 70 continues Combat Patrol with the second half of the Goliath Rockgrinder, via both sprue and paint guide. This being the biggest model released in the regular Combat Patrol magazine subscription, the paint guide is appropriately quite large. We also have the last few bits of Genestealer Cult lore and a new scenario to have our truck try and run over the other Combat Patrol subscription models. How does it handle? Let's find out!

As always, thank you to Tabletop Battles and Hachette for the opportunity to review these models, magazines, and materials.

Hobby Materials

The issue comes with the second half of the sprue of the Goliath Rockgrinder, and therefore we have the opportunity to finish building this truck (if you plan to use it in the service of the Star Children) or finish building this trukk (if it will be looted by the Orks) or finish building this Necromunda terrain (if you're a different Kevin). This issue focuses on painting up this beast, and because this is the largest single model in the regular Combat Patrol subscription, the paint guide is therefore appropriately bigger.

Credit: Keewa

The guide reminds us of the sub-assemblies we had from the last issue: the chassis, tires, front plate (Drilldozer), 2 crew members, and a Clearance Incinerator. The painting guide first warns us to cover the connection points between all these sub-assemblies with sticky tack. We then need to undercoat the model with Warhammer Paint Abaddon Black, before drybrushing the tires WHP Mechanicus Standard Grey. The chasis and Clearance Incinerator get painted WHP Administratum Grey, then shaded in WHP Agrax Earthshade, before getting additional drybrushes of Administratum Grey and Pallid Wych Flesh (the latter along the edges specifically). The crew get basecoats of Administratum Grey on their armor and undersuit, while their leather is painted Catachan Flesh. The issue calls out how to paint the crew with light skin (Wraithbone) or dark skin (Catachan Flesh). The metallics for both crew and truck are, of course, painted with Leadbelcher. The issue makes sure to note that "Safety is of the utmost importance to the crew riding a Goliath Rockgrinder - basecoat the safety railing siwth a coat of Leadbelcher". Some portions of the truck's metallics are painted in Retributor Armor in order to break up the metallic details. Lenses, dynamite, and cables are painted Mephiston Red. Lights and Fuel Canisters are painted Averland Sunset. The issue takes us through washing and shading the various components, using washes on the armor and skin of the crew members in order to show their alien nature. We are then told to edge highlight all the stuff we have painted, besides the main body of the truck. The truck itself was edge highlighted with our Palid Wych Flesh drybrush. This would give us a simple but good-looking Goliath Rockgrinder, ready to be used to throw off the oppression of The Emperor and subsequently looted by Ork Boyz. No special effects or freehand suggestions in this issue, sadly.  I'm surprised they didn't have us try and paint hazard stripes on the Rockgrinder.

Narrative Materials

We have two narrative articles this week. The first is on the main faction of the Genestealer Cults: the Cult of the Four-Armed Emperor. Having gotten their start via the Trysst Dyansty of Ghosar Quintus, they now exist across half the galaxy. The Imperium needs bodies to work its factories, mines, and other assorted industries, and doesn't pay enough attention to whether or not the skin is too purple. Since the Cult of the Four Armed Emperor is actually very good at it, the Imperium lets it continue to work until they control the undercities and subterrania, and then it is time to signal the Star Children. On that day, the Imperium finds the their weapons missing, their vehicles sabotaged, and the war is already won.

Unless, of course, something equally as inhuman from beyond the stars arrives to even the score.

Chaplain Cassius and his Ultramarines fighting Tyranids. Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

The Ghosar Quintus cult was discovered and crushed by the second-oldest Ultramarine currently roaming the stars, Chaplain Ortan Cassius, back when he was with the Deathwatch. While Cassius was able to wipe out the Genestealers, his Kill Team realized that the Trysst dynasty had shipped everywhere throughout the galaxy - and therefore spread throughout the known galaxy. Cassius would need to thus lead a new war to determine the fate of humanity.

Luckily for the Imperium, it was not something that Chaplain Cassius was unfamiliar with.

Gaming Materials

We get the 10th Edition list for the Hand of the Magus Combat Patrol, a "twisted horde of Genestealer Cultists seeking to throw off the chains of their Imperial oppressors." The issue also comes with Scenario 43: Grind all Opposition. The Genestealer Cults player gets to bring their Rockgrinder and 10 hybrids against the Opposition, which has 10 different waves to pick models from. The Opposition player starts with 3 Hearthkyn Warriors, and it goes through 3 Votann units, 3 Ork units (including the Boomdakka Snazzwagon), and four Space Marine units. The game is determined by how many waves the Genestealer player can survive. The main fun of this mission seems to be using the Deadly Demise ability to hopefully blow up the Rockgrinder and take enemy units with it.

The Final Verdict

What I said last week remains valid:  While you need both Issues 69 and 70 to finish the Rockgrinder, I believe this is the biggest and probably most versatile model in the regular issues of the magazine.  Beyond having an alternate assembly (the Goliath Truck), beyond being thematic for multiple other factions and a different game entirely, and beyond being a big truck, this model is a large, broad canvas for painting in a way that no other models in the subscription (aside from, arguably, the Helbrute or Deff Dread) are.  Additionally, the narrative articles are fun because they actually show the insidious spread of the cults and show off my main man Ortan Cassius fighting them.

This also ends the Genestealer Cults, and arguably starts more Genestealer Cultists...or as they're better known, the Imperial Guard.

Until next time, Combat Patrolers!

content:
Games Workshop has finally started releasing 11th edition Warhammer 40k codex rulebooks in earnest! The Orks, Space Marines, and terrifyingly powerful Adeptus Custodes are out, and more are on their way. Read on for Wargamer's complete 11th edition codex tracker, updated regularly with all the latest news about codex release dates, plus key FAQs to understand how your old 10th edition codexes work in the new edition.

If you're new to Games Workshop's premier sci-fi miniature wargame, our expert guide to the Warhammer 40k factions will help you get oriented in this huge sci-fi world.

  • 11th Edition codex release schedule

After a few months spooling up, Games Workshop's giant, promethium powered codex printing machine is finally chugging away for 11e! Orks, Space Marines and Adeptus Custodes are out, and there will be over 20 more codex rulebooks on the way over the next three years.

What is the next Warhammer 40k Codex release?

At the time of this update, Games Workshop hasn't announced the next Warhammer 40k Codex release. The most recent Codex release was the Adeptus Custodes on October 17, but GW hasn't revealed who's getting the next release. For the sake of the poor, suffering Astra Militarum, we hope it's them, but until the next big Warhammer preview it's anyone's guess.

Where is the 11th edition codex roadmap?

As always in the first few months of a new edition, the release schedule is full of "TBC" - to be confirmed. However, based on how GW communicated its schedules in 10th edition, the game's larger, active new audiences, and the general acceleration of marketing activity since 2023, we expect GW to release an initial 11th edition codex roadmap by December 2026.

Roadmaps normally chart out the main codex releases for a year in loose detail, with the release windows getting less specific and more mysterious towards the end - reflecting both GW's shifting production schedules, and its tendency to keep fans guessing at all times.

10th Edition codex release dates

The final 10th Edition Warhammer 40k codex was Codex: Drukhari, which went up for pre-order on September 27, 2025, and released on October 11.

In the three years of tenth edition, a whopping 30 factions received either a codex or an updated index. This includes a re-release of Index Deathwatch - which was briefly deprecated by Codex Imperial Agents - and mid-edition refreshes of both Index Chaos Daemons and Index Imperial Knights.

Of course, we're now in the era of 11th Edition - but GW has confirmed that 10th edition codexes will remain valid until each faction's new book comes along. This differs from 10th edition's launch in 2023, when all the previous codexes were invalidated by brand new, temporary index rules published for every army.

How do I redeem Warhammer 40k codex codes?

You'll find a unique Warhammer 40k codex code in the back of each printed Codex. You can register this code on your MyWarhammer account, which will in turn unlock all the datasheets and Detachments from the Codex in the Warhammer 40k app.

You can then use that data in the Battle Forge army builder. You will be limited to just one army list at a time in the app, unless you also have a Warhammer+ subscription.

Warhammer 40k codexes FAQ

Codexes are bread and butter to long time Warhammer 40,000 fans; we know what they're for, we know how they change the game, and boy oh boy do we know how much they cost.

But if you're new to the hobby, the whole concept of them can be a bit bewildering. The idea of needing another rulebook, on top of the actual rulebook, is tough enough - but buying a new one every three years? It's one of the rougher parts of the 40k hobby, and it bears a bit of explanation. Here's what codexes are, how they work, how to use them, and how they may change in the future.

What is a Warhammer 40k codex?

Alongside the core rules for Warhammer 40k, each army has its own codex where you'll find rules for all its units, the army-wide rules that give it a distinctive character, and other options you can choose from when you construct a list. They also contain artwork, lore, stories, and examples of painted armies.

What do you use the codex for in games?

During a game of Warhammer 40k - especially when you're new to the game or learning a new faction - you'll need to refer to your army's codex frequently to check its rules.

Most importantly, you need to know the stats for each unit, its weapons, and abilities. For example, you'll find yourself double checking how many inches it can move each turn, the range and power of its shooting attacks, or how effective its armor is at preventing damage. Over time, you'll know more and more of those key numbers from memory - but it's important to have the codex on hand to double check, so you don't accidentally cheat!

Codexes are also super important before the game, as they include the different Detachments you can choose for your army. These are army building choices which shape your game plan by applying different army wide buffs, as well as specialized abilities to trigger at crucial moments during the game.

Can I buy a digital or PDF version of my codex?

No, Games Workshop doesn't sell PDF versions of codexes. Since the launch of the official Warhammer 40k app in July 2020, the only official, GW supported way to view a codex's rules in digital form is to buy a copy of the physical book, then redeem its unique code to unlock it inside the app. We've written instructions on doing that - see above.

Prior to 2020, new 40k codex books were available in both printed physical and ebook formats. They were never sold as PDFs, so any codex PDF you encounter online is likely to be an unauthorized pirate copy.

How do Games Workshop's codex release dates work?

During each three year long 'edition' of Warhammer 40k, GW normally releases one new codex for each playable army in the game. Typically, they're released in groups of one or two, once every two months or so.

How and when these codexes are released can vary, depending on how fundamentally the current 'edition' has hanged the game's core rules. Because 10th Edition changed the core rules significantly in 2023, GW completely retired all 9th Edition codexes from the game, and provided a full set of free 'index' rules for each army, for fans to play with until their army's new full codex arrived.

As codexes were released, they superceded the indexes, updating rules and points, and adding new detachments that provided different ways to build an army that complete with with new abilities, enhancements, stratagems.

What about old codexes - can I use those?

As soon as an army's latest Warhammer 40k codex is released, the previous edition's rules are no longer valid in 'Matched Play' games. That means tournaments and organized play in general will always use the most up to date codex rules, and all earlier books are no longer usable.

However, many players enjoy running games of older editions, deliberately using the rules from previous editions' core rules and codexes, to play the game 'as it was then'. Your old codexes might not be tournament legal, but they don't simply disappear!

Got a burning question about your codex? You'll find a friendly and helpful community in the Wargamer Discord. To keep up with the latest news about upcoming codex releases, subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews Tenebris Somnia
content:
Arriving just in time for the last half of October, New Blood dropped the finalized version of the vaulted "FMV Survival Horror" Tenebris Somnia, teased quite a while back with a pretty impressive trailer and demo nearly two years ago. The game especially caught my eye because of New Blood itself, a publisher that's produced some of my favorite games in recent memory (Ultrakill, Fallen Aces, and FAITH), but it wasn't exactly explained how the game would combine the live-action FMV elements with the gameplay itself, which seemed to feature pixelated side-scrolling action. So when the game released earlier yesterday, I took advantage of some of the extra time I had on my hands to dive in. I figured if it didn't end up impressing me, I'd simply refund it, and if it was at least decent, I could maybe finish it over the weekend.

As I put this review together, it is currently 5:30 AM in my timezone, and I realize that I spent much of my day playing Tenebris Somnia, watching other people play Tenebris Somnia, taking a little break to do my household tasks while thinking about Tenebris Somnia, and then finally having felt that I digested the game enough, sat down to write a review about Tenebris Somnia.

The concept now of even having considered thinking of a refund is quaint.

Full Motion, Live Action, All Gas

To address perhaps the biggest thing the game made waves with, Tenebris Somnia features live action cutscenes that are primarily acted out without voice acting; while not exactly silent films, the music, sound effects, and the occasional panicked noise or gasp or growl is all that fills the space. The initial "FMV" tag was something that I think stands out as something I'm not entirely sure I'm sure is the correct tag to use, but also there really aren't many other proper ways to use them. For example, the famous trailer footage used of the demonic presence lunging at our protagonist, Julia, and in the game you'll see that same scene as well as quite a few others. The issue I've had as I sat on the concept is thinking back to FMV games like the absolutely abysmal Night Trap or the amazing X-Files game for the PS1, among many others: the FMV aspect isn't directly involved in the gameplay, but instead takes the place of cut scenes and important plot points for the game. I don't think it is wrong to call it FMV, but if you're thinking of FMV games like the above mentioned adventure/point and click style, there's a bit of a difference here.

That said, the live action scenes are amazing. The acting and cinematography show some very fun craft and consideration of how to represent the ideas or concepts without relying on dialogue, but as practical effects fan, I really have to applaud the team here for what they've managed to put together; there are some truly gnarly practical effects throughout the game that blew me away when they occurred, and I don't really want to spoil them but let's just say that the monster reveals get increasingly awesome and intricate as the game progresses, with their FMVs really selling them; the endings also make really great use of the live action juxtaposition (there are 4 endings, by the way), and by the time I was done with the game I had really come around on the mixture of pixel art gameplay and live-action horror.

Surviving the Horrors

The actual gameplay of Tenebris Somnia is that of a survival horror game, played out entirely in 2D; you can move Julia along the cardinal directions (which is to say, up, down, left, and right) in the scenes in which you control her, but there is really only the flat 2D plane of the game. You'll be doing a fair bit of backtracking in the game, as the somewhat restricted environment also plays into survival horror expectations; instead of a police station or rural, foggy city, Julia spends the game exploring a twisted version of her ex's memories, primarily taking place at a film school.

Something I found fairly of interest early on is that the game does have a fair amount of written dialogue and terminology that tells the story of what is actually going on in this alternative reality and the mystery of Julia's ex (and her own issues), but there isn't a lot of reading required to complete the game, instead often having objectives explained through visual and color cues. I know it is an odd thing to praise a game for, perhaps, but I enjoyed that the game did not rely on huge flashing signs going DO THING HERE, while instead letting the visual language and storytelling do the work and hoping the player can piece things together.

Like most survival horror games, the main gameplay loop comes down to exploration and combat, and puzzle solving. I will say that puzzles were the weakest overall aspect of the game, because many of them were simply "find a symbol/locked door/etc, find the thing that matches that, open/solve/move past the obstacle". There are some pretty fun puzzles that play into the focus on film and movies that the game has going on in the background of its concept, but overall the puzzles mostly exist to give the game something to have you "do" to excuse the back and forth exploration.

Perhaps the surprise here for me is that the combat was the star. A 2D survival horror game with good combat? I have to give that a lot more thought than I have time for at the moment to whether or not I can think of a similar experience, and frankly, survival horror game combat is often not the star of the show. At some level, it is a little funny that Julia can so easily tackle all of the horrible beasts you encounter in the game, but also, it feels pretty good and controls well, allowing even for melee combat to feel less like a last resort and more like a viable option whether or not you are running low on ammo. This especially shines in the boss fights, all of which I frankly found to be a lot of fun and quite imaginative, making great use of the vibe and concepts of the game to present the bosses as fun, challenging, but never frustrating.

Absolute Cinema

I mentioned that film and movies play a big role in Tenebris Somnia, and I wanted to touch on that in a way that won't spoil the game at all; I often find that horror games are best experienced without really knowing the plot beforehand (and perhaps that can be said of just about anything with a plot, but I digress) simply because most of the time the mystery, suspense, and conceits of horror games are wrapped up in their stories. I think perhaps no series has suffered this violence of being spoilered to hell and back than Silent Hill, and Tenebris Somnia certainly has some influence and nods to that series here that makes going in with little information valuable. Primarily, it makes playing the game again, or replaying certain scenes or attempting different endings, more meaningful; you start to notice the concepts and ideas the game was sprinkling in the whole time after your initial experience, rather than having had some loudmouth tell you them all in advance.

In that way, it's pretty clear that the team on Tenebris Somnia love movies, as if the lovingly made and weird practical effects scenes weren't key enough. But there is a lot of focus on what movies are, and what they mean, and how they are made, that permeates the game and its narrative; in a lot of ways, it tends to do so both directly and subconsciously, working in concepts of perspective, storytelling, editing, and the like into the narrative of the game (as in, what Julia is experiencing) and as a story told between the developers and their audience, who are playing and watching Julia's story. While there's always a common discussion going on between the relationship of video game and film and how they influence, react with, or even at times fight for relevance against one another, Tenebris Somnia isn't super interested in that; it seems more interested in exploring the concepts of the viewer and the viewed, and the story it wants to tell resonates with that as well. Perhaps the thing I liked about the game, aside from one of the endings which I found very fun, is that it tells a solid narrative that takes full effect of the mixed media of the game itself. Julia is a solid protagonist, and I liked playing as her as much as I liked watching her, and I found that both the "game" Julia and "movie" Julia felt coherent.

If you're in the mood for a fun new horror game to play as we move closer to Halloween, or just enjoy survival horror and fascinating indie games that take advantage of their gimmick and aesthetic to the max, then Tenebris Somnia is a very solid recommendation; I found it took me about 8 hours to fully see everything the game had to offer, but I actually think I may play through it fully again after I get some sleep and rest on the game; it's a lot of fun to play, and I'm curious to see people talking about it following the initial release wave; if you end up picking the game up, I'd love to hear your thoughts on it!
